#4646. Rare glob-eyed fish spotted in ocean’s twilight zone

Published Oct 29, 2026 2:01 PM EDT

Few deep-sea species will cause an entire research vessel’s crew to rush into the control room to catch a glimpse—but the barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma) is one of them. During the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute’s (MBARI) recent eight-day Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition, oceanographers aboard the David Packard were reunited with one of these rare, surreal creatures for the first time in nearly five years. This time, they successfully recorded the ethereal fish using a high-resolution 4K camera attached to Doc Ricketts, the ship’s remotely operated vehicle (ROV).

“Seeing a barreleye fish is a rare treat,” Steven Haddock, a MBARI senior scientist, said in the institute’s announcement. “Crew from across the ship joined the science team in the control room, mesmerized by this remarkable animal.”

M. microstoma swims through the ocean’s twilight zone, a dim region around 2,000 feet deep in the water column. “Swims” may be a bit generous, however. The barreleye fish spends most of its time drifting in place, while using its large fins to maintain stability. Acute vision is pointless in the near-dark water, so M. microstoma evolved a truly unique set of eyes. The tubular organs roll back far enough to gaze upwards through transparent tissue in its head to hunt for prey. Subtle shadows alert the fish to a target, at which point its eyes rotate forward so it can pursue the potential meal.

Biologists are also fascinated by M. microstoma eyes’ green lenses, which resemble those of the strawberry squid (Histioteuthis heteropsis). Researchers theorize the pigment allows the fish to spot bioluminescence, giving it an additional tool to maneuver through the murky depths.

MBARI marine biologists have conducted around 7,000 ROV dives over almost 40 years of ocean surveys. In the process, they’ve amassed more than 41,000 hours of video footage.. Researchers have only spotted 11 barreleye fish in all that time, and their most recent encounter occurred in 2021.

“[The barreleye fish] reminds us of the surprising ways that animals have adapted to thrive in the ocean’s midwater,” added Haddock. “So many of them survive by looking for subtle optical cues…pitting bioluminescent camouflage against increasingly sophisticated visual capabilities.”

#4645. E-quipment highlight: the highest-rated mowers on Amazon are ELECTRIC (2026)

Despite decades of market dominance, it seems like the days of loud, finicky, gas-powered mowers may finally be behind us; and I say that because – for the second year in a row! – the highest-rated lawnmowers on Amazon won’t burn a drop of gas.

The latest round of dumb oil wars are ratcheting up fuel prices everywhere while, at the same time, state and local governments continue to tightening restrictions on noise and small-engine emissions. Combined, those things probably mean that your next lawn mower is more likely to plug in than fill up, whether you like it or not. The good news is that. in addition to being quieter, safer, and not poisoning the air you breathe while you walk behind them, electric laenmowers have come a long way in terms of power and performance in just a few years. So much so, in fact, that many of the highest-rated models on Amazon, emphatic period, are electric.

In putting this list together, we looked at the average star ratings of a number of lawn mowers on Amazon, focusing on products that had at least 2,000 reviews and a four-star average or higher, and found that (like last year) battery-electric units from EGO Power, Greenworks, and Worx were among the top-rated mowers, regardless of fuel type.

Here’s the rundown, in alphabetical order (by brand).

Over the past few years, the EGO POWER+ brand has staked a claim to being the gold standard for cordless lawn equipment, thanks to its high-voltage 56V battery platform and premium build quality. The brand’s 21″ POWER+ LM2112 push mower currently carries a 4.5-star average rating from more than 2,200 Amazon reviews and an “Overall Pick” designation.

That’s no surprise, given the LM2112’s 6 ft-lbs. of cutting torque (equivalent to a 150cc ICE), and up to 35 minutes of runtime (call it a suburban yard) from the included 56V 4.0 Ah li-ion battery, three-in-one mulching, bagging and side-discharge capability. It also starts at the push of a button, folds for compact storage and skips the exhaust, maintenance, and oil changes that come along with a comparable gas mower.

With an impressive 4.2-star rating after more than 12,000 verified reviews, the Greenworks 40V 16″ push mower is in rare company among mowers of any kind on Amazon. No surprise, given that the lightweight, cordless mower weighs just 37.5 lbs. and comes with a 4.0Ah battery and charger good for up to 40 minutes of runtime, making it ideal for homeowners with smaller yards who want to ditch gas without wrestling with a heavier machine.

The Greenpower’s 16″ cutting deck is designed for (if not limited to) compact lawns, with a five-position height adjustment and a two-in-one system offering you a choice of mulching (yes) or bagging (no) your lawn clippings.

For bigger, more demanding lawns, Greenworks offers a 4.4-star push mower with a 21″ steel cutting deck that’s powered by an 80V brushless motor and ships with a pair of 2.0 Ah batteries good for up to 40 minutes of runtime with both batteries. Three-in-one functionality for mulching, bagging, or side discharge is included, too, along with push-button starting, seven-position height adjustment, and a rapid charger that can get it back to work in about 30 minutes.

WORX’s 40V 17″ Power Share mower is another strong example of how electric lawn care can be both practical and affordable. The WG743 mates a pair of 20V, 4.0 Ah batteries to deliver 40V of power, and those same batteries work across the brand’s broader Power Share lineup of tools – a lineup that includes string trimmers, power drills, and more.

The WORX mower’s standout feature, though, is its “IntelliCut” technology that works a bit like traction control in your car, automatically increasing torque when the mower hits thicker grass (more traction) and backing off when it doesn’t need the extra power (when it detects wheelspin – or, in this case, cutting head spin). Factor in an intentionally lightweight design, seven-position cutting-height adjustment, and the de rigueur options for mulching or bagging, and you’ve got a versatile little mower for keeping a smaller lawn in shape.

I just ordered the 60v super recycler with delivery on Tuesday. A friend bought one this year and he raved about its dual power button, commercial bag system that throws grass to rear of bagger for complete fill up and full aluminum deck, 3 year warranty. My 20 year old skil 18v tools still perform like new with newer higher powered batteries, along with my 20v updated black and decker tool assortment. Next year giving my like new 15 year old snow blower 2 stage to son buying a Toro 60v 2 stage same as the gas model except battery powered. My gas power washer stays as with a 6 car concrete driveway, 2000 sq ft patio a professional ss surface cleaner requires long running powerful performance.

#4644. Have You Ever Had Sex That Felt Scary?

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

In 2014, the White House Task Force to Protect Students from Sexual Assault found that 20 percent of college women get raped as undergraduates. The report generated controversy. That many? Really? The controversy spurred research. Three years later, a large study by investigators at many U.S. colleges and universities concluded the statistic was “reasonably accurate.” (Muehlenhard, 2017)

During the decade since that Task Force, many colleges, universities, and the military have instituted rape-prevention programs that inform young women of their risk, warn against getting drunk at parties, and encourage “designated sober” bystanders to intervene if they see trouble. Those programs have reduced women’s risk of sexual assault in higher education and the military by 50 percent.

Rape-prevention programs have also spotlighted the fact that some problematic young-adult sexual interactions don’t constitute sexual assault, but are still unwanted and scary. Recently, Indiana University researchers investigated who experiences scary sex and why.

The researchers surveyed 721 undergraduates, average age 19, at Indiana University, 49 percent women, 49 percent men, 2 percent other, divided roughly evenly among first-, second-, third-, and fourth-year students. Almost 80 percent were heterosexual, with 12 percent bisexual, 5 percent lesbian/gay, and 4 percent transgender or gender non-binary. Half were single, half in relationships. Completing the 20-minute survey entered them in a lottery for $100 gift cards. (Herbenick, 2025)

Almost one-third of survey respondents (31 percent) reported at least one sexual experience they called scary. Three-quarters of them (75 percent) were women, 21 percent were men, and 5 percent were transgender or gender non-binary.

The researchers grouped scary experiences into seven categories:

This is not the only study to delve into frightening sex. Two pilot reports by Indiana University researchers showed that 25 percent of women and 10 percent of men reported sometimes feeling scared during sex. (Herbenick, 2019, 2022) Those studies inspired this larger one.

Scary sex may include activities that are standard elements of bondage-discipline-sado-masochism (BDSM): restraint, rough play, and sacrifice of control. But in mutually pleasurable BDSM, the players negotiate their play beforehand. They agree to every move, and everyone knows exactly how the play will unfold. They also adopt “safe words” to stop the action if anyone feels uncomfortable or scared.

Across all categories, some participants of every gender and sexual preference reported feeling scared. But overwhelmingly, they were women and sexual and gender minorities—and their fear was inspired by male partners. In other words, the problem is out-of-control young men. Parents, older siblings, college staff, and mental health professionals should tell young men repeatedly and bluntly that they better control themselves or they risk prison.

What makes men lose control? Usually alcohol. Although today’s young adults drink less than previous generations, alcohol continues to fuel reckless behavior. Anyone who deals with young people should tell them repeatedly and bluntly that alcohol intoxication may embroil them in situations they would rather avoid. Beer commercials say “drink responsibly.” To prevent scary sex, a better message would be “just one drink if any, no more.”

Young adults experiment with both sex and drugs. We’ve all been there and know that some of those experiments play with fire. To avoid getting burned, young adults should take responsibility for their safety by:

Some might call this victim-blaming. It’s not. It’s taking adult responsibility for personal safety. That’s prudent—and as this study shows, unfortunately necessary.

Herbenick, D et al. “‘I Just Really Didn’t Know What I Was Walking Into,’: Scary Sexual Experiences in a Campus-Representative Survey of Undergraduate Students,” Journal of Sex and Marital Therapy (2025) 51:58. Doi: 10.1080/0092623X.2024.2433102.

Herbenick, D et al. “‘It Was Scary, But Then It Was Kind of Exciting’: Young Women’s Experiences with Choking During Sex,” Archives of Sexual Behavior (2022) 51:1103. Doi: 10.1007/s10508-021-02049-x.

Herbenick, D et al. “Feeling Scared During Sex: Findings from a U.S. Probability Sample of Women and Men Ages 14 to 60,” Journal of Sex and Marital Therapy (2019) 45:424. Doi: 10.1080/0092623x.2018.1549634.

Kilimnik, CD, et al. “Undergraduate Students’ Definitions of Sexual Violence Labels Across the Rise of the #MeToo Movement,” Psychology of Women Quarterly (2024) 48:430. Doi: 10.1177/03616843241239634.

Klein, LB, et al. “Sexual and Relationship Violence Among LGBTQ+ College Students: A Scoping Review,” Trauma, Violence, and Abuse (2023) 24:2196. Doi: 10.1177/15248380221089981.

Muehlenhard, CL et al. “Evaluating the One-In-Five Statistic: Women’s Risk of Sexual Assault While in College,” Journal of Sex Research (2017) 54:549. Doi: 10.1080/00224499.2017.1295014.

Wilson, LC et at. “Meta-Analysis of the Prevalence of Unacknowledged Rape,” Trauma, Violence, and Abuse (2016) 17:149. Doi: 10.1177/1524838015576391.

#4643. MIT develops robot that slithers through intestines like a snake

Published Oct 29, 2026 3:10 PM EDT

Worms are usually the last thing someone wants in their gut. Just ask this unfortunate Alaskan bear recently spotted with several multi-foot long tapeworms hanging out of its butt. However, a  new type of gut-crawling worm being designed by engineers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), may actually be here to help.

Their soft robot, called BIOSENTER, is designed to autonomously inch through the crowded, cramped, and coiled small intestine, contracting and extending its body much like an earthworm or snake. It does that by alternately pumping air through four inflatable chambers on either side of its hollow body. Once inside, the wiggly worm-bot can snap photos, administer drugs, and even take small biopsy samples. It can also slither into the intestine via a person’s mouth or rear-end all by itself.

Horrifying as all of this might sound, the team behind it says the robot could offer a faster, less labor-intensive alternative to double-balloon enteroscopy, the current standard for examining  the small intestine. And with intestinal diseases and cancers on the rise, any methods to detect issues early could have potentially life-saving results. The team published details about the robot this week in the journal Science Robotics.

The small intestine is a particularly challenging place to run diagnoses. Though it can measure 20 feet long, it’s tightly coiled up in a cramped part of the abdomen. It is also hemmed in by the stomach and colon, which can make it difficult to reach.  But bleeding, lessons, and blockages can develop in the small intestine which can lead to big problems if left untreated. Currently, the most common way to examine the organ is double-balloon enteroscopy. Healthcare workers repeatedly inflate and deflate two balloons to work a scope through the digestive tract. The method works, but it’s slow and requires constant hands-on attention.

“The fundamental challenge that we’re trying to overcome is how to evaluate that 20-to-25-foot segment of the small intestine in a way that can be more automated,” Giovanni Traverso, an MIT mechanical engineer and  study-co-author, said in a statement.

The team turned to nature for a solution: snakes. These scaly reptiles move by alternating contracting muscles on either side of their body. Aside from offering protection, their scaly bodies also give them extra traction as they slither. The MIT researchers looked at this natural byproduct of evolution and saw a design that could work well in the narrow, slippery corridors of the human GI tract.

With the snake inspiration in mind, the team built a soft, rubbery robot with a hollow body. Its worm-like frame measures about 3.7 inches in length with a half inch diameter. These dimensions make it compact enough to travel through the small intestine, as well as other narrow passages in the body, like the esophagus. BIOSENTER has four inflatable chambers arranged along either side of its tubular body.  These chambers inflate and deflate in alternating combinations, which is how it moves forewarn and bends to change directions. Keeping with the snake theme, the robot’s exterior is fitted with a textured, scale-like coating that improves its traction.

Additionally, the worm has expandable sections built in its head and tail inspired by a type of Japanese origami called kirigami, that uses cuts as well as folds. These inflatable segments alternately grip and release the intestinal wall, anchoring the robot so it can pull itself forward. BIOSENTER’s hollowed out body houses a variety of tools: cameras for imaging, a sprayer for drug delivery, and tiny clippers to take tissue samples. The entire thing is tethered to an external system via cable. Though it’s meant to move mostly autonomously, healthcare workers can also control BIOSENTER through a handheld device reminiscent of an Xbox controller.

“By using kirigami sleeves to enhance surface friction, the robot can generate localized tissue engagement traction for locomotion without relying on excessive stretching of the delicate small intestinal tissue,” added MIT graduate student Ahmad Mujtaba Jebran..

The team tested the robot on several sedated,  living pigs, because their GI tract anatomy resembles the kind humans have. During testing, BIOSENTER navigated the pigs’ intestines for 11 minutes, capturing real-time images, collecting small tissue biopsies, and delivering fluid to specific locations.

BIOSENTER notably isn’t the first gut-crawling robot. In 2021, a team from the University of Macau in China designed a prototype robot inspired by an African spider that moves using a cartwheel motion. In that case, the robot is injected via a vitamin sized capsule and traverses the GI tract (including the small intestine) via a magnetic field. Rather unglamorously, the spider bot is expelled by pooping.

#4642. Battery electric, solar-powered reefer units reach their first customers

The first regular production solar-powered electric trailer refrigeration unit (TRU) in Australia has hit the road with a real customer. Family-owned transport giant Wickham Freight Lines took delivery of the revolutionary reefer just this week.

Refrigerated trailers (reefers) are critical for hauling fresh food and flowers from the farm to your local market — the problem is that they pollute like crazy, powered by high sulfur, red-dye diesel-powered generators that run around the clock, even if the truck pulling them is fully electric. That constant diesel burn spews CO₂ and NOx into industrial and residential areas alike, and contributes significantly to fleets’ carbon emissions and noise pollution at a time when a number of municipalities are moving to regulate both.

It is, as they say, “a real problem,” but Sunswap Endurance cracked it with a solar-powered reefer that can keep food and pharmaceuticals cold in transit without burning a drop of diesel fuel – and now, they have real customers.

One of Australia’s largest privately owned trucking companies, Wickham Freight Lines decided to purchase the Sunswap Endurance solar trailer units following an initial trial, running from Sydney to Brisbane and back this past summer on a route covering a total of 1,670 km (~1,040 miles) over more than 30 hours of driving.

After Wickham’s drivers finished the round trip with over 65% of the battery’s capacity still left, the purchase was a no-brainer.

“I put the Sunswap Endurance into the fleet and told the team to stretch it — treat it as a normal unit,” explains Graham Keogh, director at Wickham Freight Lines. “We were genuinely impressed. I’m a true believer. I love the technology and I’m not a true tech person whatsoever. You can just see that it’s a winner … the performance, reliability and operational savings were beyond what we expected. For a business like ours, running a large fleet across the east coast, with a heavy focus on refrigerated and cold chain freight, this technology makes real commercial sense.”

Sunswap Endurance first showed their new solar reefer unit at HVIA TruckShowX in Hunter Valley this May past. It’s compelling, insultingly simple technology and I, for one, hope this customer delivery is just the first of many. Let us know what you think of these guys, in the comments.

Solar powered refrigeration truck looks like a natural combination. Cost of the solar is offset somewhat by not needing diesel tank, motor, and generator. Majority of savings probably come form not needing constant refueling (fuel + labor), or in not needing to overhaul the engine periodically.

I would be very interested in knowing how quickly the system pays for itself.

#4641. Gamma-ray burst is one of the brightest in decades

Published Oct 29, 2026 4:15 PM EDT

A gamma-ray burst (GRB) that has confounded astronomers is one of the brightest cosmic light shows in the past 20 years. Although the cosmic explosion first appeared inexplicably weak, researchers now believe it actually shot about one billion years’ worth of solar energy into the cosmos through a beam no thicker than a pencil.

“We see hundreds of GRBs every year, but the oddballs are the most informative ones,” said Roberto Ricci, a radioastronomer at Italy’s National Institute of Astrophysics.

Ricci and his colleague’s findings are detailed in a study recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. On March 10, NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope observed a burst later classified as GRB 260310A. Gamma-ray bursts most frequently occur in the aftermath of a massive star’s collapse. When this happens, powerful jets of matter launch into space close to the speed of light. These jets collide with cosmic gas, which generates afterglows seen across visible light, radio waves, and X-rays.

While GRB 260310A’s flash of light lasted less than one minute, astronomers noted it seemed to produce strangely little energy. This changed within only a few hours, as GRB 260310A’s afterglow brightened so much that it briefly outshone its host galaxy. A few weeks later, the GRB’s X-ray emissions brightened again and then remained observable for months.

“At first, I thought another X-ray source was contaminating our observations. But the brightening really came from the afterglow,” recalled study co-author and astronomer Yu-Han Yang.

Further observations using an international array of observatories and telescopes later confirmed a supernova had indeed prompted a GRB. Early signs indicated that its jet was pointed away from Earth, but while the gamma-ray readings were comparatively basic, both its visible and X-ray measurements ranked among the top one percent in brightness. GRB 260310A also fell within the top five percent for recorded radio brightness. After reviewing the data, astronomers finally realized what was happening.

“We looked at it from a side angle,” explained Yang. “As the jet slowed down, its light became visible over a wider range of angles, allowing us to probe the jet’s shape, from its outer edges toward its inner core.”

Yang compared most GRB observations to looking directly at a flashlight. Although the light is brightest from that perspective, the beam may appear dimmer if it is viewed from further away. Most GRB modeling is calibrated from events detected from a direct vantage point, but GRB 260310A was different.

“This burst gave us a chance to look beyond that glare,” said Yang.

Astronomers theorize that GRB 260310A may have originated from a jet featuring a very narrow, energized core encompassed by wider, slower outflows. If true, the early afterglow hypothetically traces back to the jet’s wings, while the brightening X-ray phase came from the thin core.

Although it took a moment to decipher, GRB 260310A offers a rarely seen window into a gamma-ray burst. Such opportunities are rare, but the team hopes to find more in the near future using even more powerful tools like the recently completed Vera Rubin Observatory.

“We could explain individual features of this burst, but fitting them all into the same picture proved much harder,” added Ricci.

#4640. Why your favorite candy tastes different now

Published Oct 30, 2026 9:03 AM EDT

It’s candy—I mean, Halloween—season. But, I mean, let’s be real: The two are kind of interchangeable at this point. But have you ever bitten into your favorite candy bar only to think, “This really doesn’t taste the way it used to?”

Well, it turns out, you might be onto something. Candy companies really do sneakily change their recipes. Our taste buds also change as we get older. So what’s really going on here? Are candy companies changing their recipes or do we just taste things differently now? To find out, Popular Science’s Ask Us Anything podcast took a deep dive into the surprisingly complicated science of candy.

Ask Us Anything answers your most outlandish, mind-burning questions—from the everyday things you’ve always wondered to the bizarre things you never thought to ask. So, yes, you really should wear sunscreen every day and no, you don’t need to worry about Yellowstone blowing up. If you have a question for us, send us a note. Nothing is too silly or simple.

This episode is based on the Popular Science article “Candy now tastes different. It’s not just you.”

Listen and follow Ask Us Anything on your favorite podcast platform:

Spotify | Apple Podcasts | YouTube | Or wherever you get your podcasts.

Sarah Durn: Halloween is right around the corner, and you know what that means: lots and lots of candy: Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups, Snickers, Kit Kats, Hershey’s chocolate bars. Whether you’re stocking up for trick-or-treaters or secretly buying a bag just for yourself, there’s something about Halloween that makes us crave our favorite childhood sweets.

But have you ever unwrapped a piece of candy you used to love as a kid, taken a bite, and thought, “Wait a second, this doesn’t taste like I remember it.” Maybe the chocolate tastes a little different, maybe the peanut butter filling isn’t quite as creamy, or maybe that candy bar just doesn’t hit the way it used to.

So what’s going on? Have candy companies been quietly changing the recipes of our childhood favorites, or is it possible that the candy hasn’t changed at all, and it’s actually our taste buds that are different?

Welcome to Ask Us Anything from the editors of Popular Science, where we answer your questions about our weird world, from, “Why don’t humans have tails?” to, “Why do dogs tilt their heads?” No question is too strange or simple. I’m Sarah Durn, an editor at Popular Science.

Laura Baisas: And I’m Laura Baisis, news editor at Popular Science.

SD: Here at PopSci, we’re always pondering quirky questions.

LB: And this week we’re wondering, why doesn’t candy taste as good as it used to? Sarah, is it really that companies are secretly changing the recipes for our favorite childhood treats?

SD: Candy, I know, candy companies really do change their recipes, and a lot of times they don’t even have to say so.

LB: Seriously? So, like, my beloved Milky Way could be completely different from the one that I ate when I was nine?

SD: Potentially. Companies can make tiny changes to their recipes that are almost impossible to notice, but over decades, those tiny little changes can really add up.

LB: Okay, so we’re not just imagining things.

SD: Not necessarily, but there’s another twist. Our taste buds also change as we get older, so the candy might be different, but so are we.

LB: Okay. But so who’s really to blame here, Big Candy on one side or my ever-aging taste buds on the other?

LB: Now, before we unwrap this mystery, we want to know, what questions are circling in your brain?

If there’s something you’ve always wanted to know, submit your question by clicking the “Ask Us” link at popsci.com/ask. Again, that’s popsci.com/ask, and click the “Ask Us” link.

SD: We can’t wait to hear your questions.

LB: We’ll be right back after a quick break to find out what’s really happening to our favorite candy.

SD: And stick around to the end, because we’re gonna be joined by a very special guest, Jack Bishop from America’s Test Kitchen.

LB: Yes, America’s Test Kitchen. What are we gonna ask him?

SD: Well, Jack has spent decades testing recipes and figuring out what makes food taste good, so we’re gonna put his taste buds to the test and find out what he thinks about his favorite childhood candies.

LB: Okay, now I’m officially hungry and excited.

And we’re back. Okay, Laura, before we get into whether our favorite candies have actually changed, I have a very important question for you: What was your favorite Halloween candy growing up?

LB: Oh, okay, before I reveal my top choice, I will say I love Dots.

LB: …so much so that my, my little nextdoor neighbors will save any Dots that they get while trick-or-treating for me just because I mentioned liking them one day.

SD: Aw, that’s, that’s really sweet, and I would never have shared my Halloween candy with you.

LB: But honestly, if I have to pick an all-time favorite, I’m gonna go with what I hinted at earlier, the Milky Way.

LB: They’re just, like, that perfect combination of flavors, so they never really get boring. It’s not just one note.

SD: Okay. Yeah. So I was obsessed with all Halloween candy. Like, lost-several-teeth-in-Laffy-Taffy-level obsessed. I would go trick-or-treating, come home with this absolutely enormous haul of candy, and then keep it all in a pillowcase under my bed.

SD: Uh-huh. And I would ration it out over the course of a year.

Sometimes I would still have Halloween candy left when the next Halloween rolled around.

SD: I know. I was basically running, like, a little candy warehouse under my bed. But devastatingly, once mice got into it, and that was… It was not, not the smartest hiding spot. But my brothers and sisters didn’t know where I had hid it, so I guess it evens out.

Yeah. But my favorite candy was probably Nerds. And now as an adult, I recently discovered Nerds Gummy Clusters.

LB: We’re actually gonna be handing those out this year.

SD: Oh my God, you guys are gonna be so popular.

SD: Oh my gosh. Okay. But all of this got me thinking about all the other candies I loved as a kid because there are definitely some that just don’t taste the way I remember.

And as it turns out, there’s a pretty good reason for that.

LB: Okay. Perfect. Let’s, let’s get into it. Are candy companies really messing with our childhood favorites?

SD: They are, 1000 percent. And one of the biggest recent controversies actually involves one of the most iconic Halloween candies, Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups.

SD: I know. Me too. So earlier this year, Brad Reese, the grandson of H.B. Reese, the inventor of Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups, publicly criticized Hershey, the company that makes the candy.

SD: Yeah, it’s kinda wild that there are family candy empires, but, you know, of course there are.

Anyhow, Brad was upset about changes to some of the company’s candy products. Specifically, he pointed to products that use things like compound coatings instead of milk chocolate or peanut butter-style cream instead of actual peanut butter.

LB: So in candy making, what exactly is a compound coating?

SD: It’s a chocolate-like coating that can use vegetable fats in place of some of the cocoa butter you’d find in traditional chocolate, and those substitutions can make a difference in how a candy tastes and feels in your mouth.

LB: The phrase chocolate-like kind of raises a red flag there.

LB: Okay, but here’s the really important question. Did they actually change Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups?

SD: According to Hershey, no. The company says the original Reese’s Peanut Butter Cup recipe hasn’t changed, but it acknowledges that some other Reese’s products, different shapes and sizes and newer varieties, can have different formulations.

LB: Oh, so the classic peanut butter cup shape might be the same, but the other Reese’s candies, like the popular pumpkins or Christmas tree shapes, aren’t necessarily made the same way.

SD: Yes, at least that’s the distinction the company is making. But this isn’t just about Reese’s. Candy companies have been adjusting their recipes for years, and to understand why, Popular Science spoke with Dr. Richard Hartel, a food scientist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, and he explained that one of the biggest reasons companies change their recipes is pretty straightforward: money.

SD: Yep. Candy manufacturers are a business, and when the price of ingredients goes up, they have a pretty strong incentive to find cheaper alternatives.

But those substitutions aren’t always obvious. Take caramel, for example.

SD: Yes, same. So traditionally, caramel might be made using whole milk and milk fat. But a manufacturer could decide to replace those ingredients with skim milk and a different kind of fat, like vegetable oil or coconut oil.

They might also replace some milk proteins with whey proteins.

SD: Potentially, but it can also change the flavor and texture of the final candy. Because even if two ingredients serve a similar purpose in a recipe, that doesn’t mean they’re gonna taste exactly the same.

LB: Right, and I imagine butter and vegetable oil don’t produce exactly the same caramel just because of chemistry.

You know, it’s like vegan or regular cooking. It’s similar, but different.

SD: Yeah. No, exactly. And the same thing can happen with chocolate. A company might reduce the amount of cocoa in a product while still keeping enough to meet the legal requirement for calling it “chocolate.”

LB: So there are legal requirements for calling it chocolate, kind of like with beer?

SD: There are, yeah. The FDA has what’s called standards of identity for certain foods. Basically, these are rules that determine what ingredients a product needs to contain or how it needs to be made to legally use a particular name. So you can’t necessarily just throw some brown colored sugar and oil together and call it milk chocolate.

LB: So it’s kind of similar to that question of if almond milk can really be called “milk.” Yes. Yeah, I guess it is kind of assuring that there are some sort of standards here.

SD: Oh, yeah. No, those standards still leave manufacturers, though, room to adjust the recipes. And if a company changes its ingredients while staying within those legal requirements, it generally doesn’t have to make some big public announcement or even change their ingredient list.

LB: Right, so there’s not gonna be a big press release saying, “Attention candy lovers, we’ve slightly reduced the cocoa content of your favorite chocolate bar.”

SD: Exactly, and that’s part of what makes this whole thing so sneaky. Because according to Hartel, some of these recipe changes are so subtle that even trained testers might not notice them.

LB: Really? So like even those lucky people whose job it is to literally taste things?

SD: Yep. Imagine you have a candy bar, you know, you’ve eaten your whole life. One year the company makes a tiny adjustment to the recipe. You probably don’t notice. The next year they make another tiny adjustment. Again, you probably don’t notice.

But if you keep doing that over 10 years or 20 years…

LB: Okay, so that explains why a candy bar might taste different now. But here’s what I’m wondering. If people notice these changes and don’t like them, why don’t companies just go back to the original recipes?

SD: Yeah, well that brings us to one of the most famous disasters in the history of food marketing: New Coke.

SD: So back in 1985, Coca-Cola decided to change its signature soda formula, and the company had actually done taste testing beforehand. In blind taste tests, people often preferred sweeter Pepsi over Coke. So Coca-Cola introduced a new sweeter version of its drink.

LB: Which as we now know, people famously hated.

SD: Hated it. And it’s all because of something called the Pepsi paradox. Basically, there’s a difference between tasting a tiny sip of something and actually consuming an entire serving. A sweeter drink might win in a quick sip test, but that doesn’t necessarily mean people want to drink a whole can.

LB: Right. That makes sense. Like if one bite of something is super sweet, it might be delicious—

LB: —but after 10 bites you might be completely over it.

SD: Yeah, and that’s a big challenge for food companies because just because a new recipe performs well in a taste test doesn’t mean consumers will actually prefer it in their everyday lives.

And with New Coke there was another huge factor.

LB: Okay. If it’s not money, I’m gonna guess it’s nostalgia.

SD: Nostalgia. People were attached to the original Coca-Cola. It wasn’t just about how the soda tasted. It was about the memories and feelings associated with it.

LB: All right, and that brings us right back to Halloween candy.

SD: Yeah. When you eat a Reese’s Peanut Butter Cup or a Hershey’s bar, you’re not necessarily just tasting chocolate and sugar and peanut butter.

LB: You might also be remembering the fun of trick-or-treating as a kid, dumping your candy all over the living room floor and trading with your siblings.

SD: Or in my case, hiding an entire year’s supply of candy under my bed.

LB: Hey, I now think it’s very important to have a secret candy bunker.

SD: Look, I concur. And that brings us to another important part of this mystery because even if a candy company hasn’t changed its recipe at all, there’s still something else that could be changing.

SD: Us. Our sense of taste isn’t necessarily the same throughout our lives.

As we get older, our ability to perceive flavors can change, and one reason is that our taste buds don’t regenerate quite as quickly as they used to.

LB: So even if I’m eating a Milky Way, I might experience it differently now.

SD: Right, even if it’s the same exact Milky Way. And it’s not just aging. Our environment and experiences also affect how we perceive taste.

So the way you experience a Milky Way today might be different from the way you experienced it as a kid, even if the recipe is identical.

LB: Okay, so with this mystery, we’ve now got two possible culprits: the candy companies are changing the recipes, and our taste buds are changing too.

SD: And both things can be true at the same time, which makes it difficult to know whether your beloved Milky Way or addictive Nerds actually taste different or whether you just remember it tasting different.

LB: So basically, no matter how much we want to, we’re never getting that exact childhood Halloween candy experience back, no matter how much we try.

SD: I know, but there’s a little good news. Candy companies do sometimes listen when people complain about changes. In fact, Hershey has announced plans to bring back older recipes for some of its products, including certain miniature Easter candies.

LB: Okay, that helps. So there’s some hope.

SD: There is, but Hershey will still experiment with new formulas for other products, so I wouldn’t expect every candy to suddenly taste exactly the way it did in 1998.

SD: But here’s the big takeaway. If you’ve bitten into your favorite childhood candy and thought, “This isn’t as good as it used to be,” you might actually be onto something.

Manufacturers really do change the recipes. Sometimes those changes are tiny, and sometimes they accumulate over decades, but our own taste perception changes too. So the answer to whether candy tastes different now is—

SD: It really is. But before we wrap up this very sweet episode, there’s one thing I want to get to the bottom of because we spent this whole episode talking about how our favorite childhood candies might be changing, but what would someone who tastes food for a living think?

LB: I feel like we need to bring in the expert here.

SD: Me too, and luckily, we got a pretty great one. After the break, we’re gonna be joined by Jack Bishop from America’s Test Kitchen.

LB: Excellent. Love America’s Test Kitchen.

And we’re back with Jack Bishop. Jack is the senior content advisor at America’s Test Kitchen, where he’s been part of the team since the very beginning, starting with the launch of Cook’s Illustrated in 1993. He’s also the tasting lab expert on America’s Test Kitchen and Cook’s Country, which means he’s spent decades putting food to the test.

Jack, thank you so much for joining us on Popular Science’s Ask Us Anything podcast.

Jack Bishop: It’s great to be here, Sarah. Thanks for asking me.

SD: Oh, we’re so excited to have you. So Jack, throughout today’s episode, we’ve been investigating whether our favorite childhood candies really taste different than they used to, and I want to start with a personal question.

Was there a candy you absolutely loved growing up that just doesn’t quite taste as good to you today?

JB: —that’s pretty much true for most candies, especially I was a child of the ’60s and ’70s, and so candies were bigger back then. In my mind, the biggest difference is the caramel isn’t as gooey as it used to be when I was a kid.

JB: When you would bite into a Snickers bar, it was almost like a cheese pull. You know, you’d get this great pull, and I feel like that doesn’t happen anymore.

SD: And given your knowledge of food generally, why do you think Snickers taste different?

JB: You know, it’s hard to say because you do the label reading, and it only gets you so far.

JB: —you know, you can tell by the order of the ingredients. If that changes, that could be a real sign. You know, if something has gone up in the ingredient list, that likely means there’s more of it, because ingredients are listed in the order of sort of weight. You know, they’re just using lower quality ingredients in order to keep costs down.

I mean, that’s the overall trend in what I would call supermarket candy.

JB: Is cost is such a big issue, and so many of the inputs have gotten so expensive. And so, you know, using less of the expensive ingredient, switching out, you know, a moderately priced ingredient for a really cheap ingredient. Those are all strategies that could be used to control cost, but they’re not necessarily gonna make something tastier.

SD: Yeah. Yeah, and if, you know, a listener is listening to this and they feel like one of their favorite candies has changed since they were growing up, what would you suggest? How would they go about testing that?

JB: I should start by saying I think taste memories are powerful but unreliable.

JB: So what I mean by that is I can make a certain recipe, and the house fills with an aroma, like I’m thinking of like my grandmother’s lasagna, and if like my brother or sister walks in, it’s like we’re back in my grandmother’s kitchen, and, you know, I’m eight, and my sister’s seven, and my brother’s five again. The food is really triggering powerful emotions.

JB: But, you know, we misremember stuff, and it’s really hard to remember, well, how sweet was this?

JB: Right? How chocolatey was this? Was this really peanut buttery, or have my tastes just changed? And I know for me, you know, I now like 85 percent cacao chocolate.

Well, I didn’t like that as a kid. And so that will color perceptions of things I did eat when I was a kid, and is it not as good as it used to be, or do I not like that anymore? Unless you can get a time machine and somebody can send you a candy bar from, you know, 1972 or whatever year you’d like to go back to, you’re relying on your memory, and your memory’s a little fickle when it comes to food.

SD: Yeah, and we’ve actually been talking a bit in this episode about Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups because they’ve been at the center of this whole conversation about changing candy recipes, and I know America’s Test Kitchen actually has its own recipe for homemade peanut butter cups. So I’m curious, what makes a really great peanut butter cup? Is there something the homemade version can get right that a store-bought candy might not?

JB: Fewer ingredients and better ingredients. So, you know, if you read the label on a Reese’s Peanut Butter Cup, it’s a pretty long ingredient list. Our homemade version starts with milk chocolate and creamy peanut butter that you enrich with a little bit of butter, a little bit of salt, and a little bit of confectioner sugar ‘cause the confectioner sugar will incorporate into the sugar without giving you any sort of grittiness, and that’s it.

It’s really just creamy peanut butter that’s a little sweeter and a little saltier and a little richer than it is straight out of the jar layered with melted chocolate, and you need, don’t need to anything more than put the chocolate in the microwave, 50 percent power to gently melt it, and then you can actually build them.

The easiest way to do this is in a mini muffin tin.

JB: And you can get little liners, and you sort of pipe a layer of chocolate, pipe a layer of peanut butter, and then finish with a layer of chocolate. So the chocolate’s not completely enrobing the peanut butter, but it’s the neatest, easiest way to do it at home, and it eats like…

Well, I won’t say it eats like a Reese’s Peanut Butter Cup ‘cause it’s so much better.

SD: Well, Jack, thank you so much for joining us. I need to go make peanut butter cups apparently. And Jack, if listeners wanna know more about what you’re up to in America’s Test Kitchen, where should they go?

JB: Sure. We’ve got, you know, tastings of milk chocolate, dark chocolate, white chocolate, and you can find all of those results at americastestkitchen.com.

SD: Great. Thank you so much for making the time, Jack.

LB: Wow, I love him so much. And even though I can’t cook to save my life, I kind of want to try that homemade peanut butter cup recipe.

SD: I know, me too. We’ll link it in the show notes.

And if you like our show, leave us a rating and a review.

SD: What’s your favorite candy? Let us know in the comments. Our producer is Alan Haburchak, and this week’s episode was based on an article written for Popular Science by Andrew Coletti.

LB: Thank you, team, thank you, candy, and thank you everyone for listening.

SD: And one more time, if you want something you’ve always wondered about explained on a future episode, go to popsci.com/ask and click the “Ask Us” link. Until next time, keep the questions coming, and may your candy stay mice-free.

LB: I’m still sad about Baby Sarah’s candy stash.

#4639. A Famous Case of Shared Eyewitness 'Memory'

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

In previous posts of the Forensic View, we have seen that eyewitness memory, while frequently convincing to jurors and the public, is frequently and sometimes fabulously unreliable. But what happens when our confidence in reported eyewitness information is essentially “wired in parallel,” shared among different people who may, with repetition, put their own stamps on the information?

In 1914, during the First World War, these processes resulted in strongly held beliefs that Russian troops were coming.

All histories of that terrible conflict discuss the importance of Russian military operations in Eastern Europe. The hardships and horrifying casualty counts of that very harsh campaign are well attested.

But none of that happened in Scotland, where tens of thousands of entirely imaginary Russians were firmly believed to have turned up anyway.

The whole mess seems to have started on August 27th, 1914, when there was a long delay in the railway service linking London and Liverpool. Somebody, perhaps in an ill-advised attempt to boost morale, explained to somebody else that this was due to the diversion of trains which were transporting thousands of Russian troops, who had landed in Scotland, to reinforce the Western Front.

Word spread. These Russians’ route was allegedly very specific; they had crossed the Arctic Sea to Norway, then traveled by steamship to Aberdeen, and from there were being carried by special troop trains to the Channel ports.

Now, prior frameworks for understanding strongly influence our ability to remember and interpret information (Bransford & Johnson, 1973), even when those frameworks are completely incorrect, and the resulting memories and interpretations are therefore complete rubbish (Sharps, 2024; Sharps & Price-Sharps, 2026). However, when such frameworks, accurate or not, are filled with plausible feature-intensive detail, people may be increasingly inclined to believe them (Sharps, 2022, 2024); and the specificity of these peripatetic Russians’ itineraries helped to convince people of their absolute reality.

Additional details followed. Witnesses had supposedly seen Russians stamping snow off their boots at railway stations (Pennell, 2015). Makes sense—Russia has a lot of snow. Granted, how those troops managed to maintain that snow on their boots all the way to Edinburgh in August is quite a mystery (Tuchman, 1962); but since the story included the very specific detail of an imaginary railway porter who had swept up the imaginary snow, who was going to argue with this imaginary account?

Very reliable people had supposedly seen these Russians. An Oxford professor knew a colleague who’d been summoned as a Russian translator, and a Scots army officer had seen their big fur caps and, believe it or not, their bows and arrows. Why these Russian troops lacked modern weapons remains unexplained, but with enough popular momentum behind the story, people believed it anyway. The people of the time were under the extraordinary stress of horrible new types of warfare that produced casualty rates virtually beyond comprehension for that day—and it has been shown that when people are under stress, they are more likely to ignore evidentiary flaws in accounts (Sharps et al., 2013; Sharps, 2024).

Evidently, this psychological effect extended to snow in August and 20th-century Russian infantrymen armed like Robin Hood.

A Scots landowner personally reported 125,000 Russians marching across his property (Tuchman, 1962), which seems a bit low when 500,000 imaginary Russians were originally reported; but gradually these imaginary numbers dropped down to an equally imaginary 70,000 or 80,000, which presumably made people feel more confident about the realism of the whole imaginary business.

Some actual history became involved in this mess, as well. The naval battle of Heligoland Bight, which had nothing whatsoever to do with Russians, was explained as some form of weird diversion to cover the sea transport of these imaginary forces to Belgium (Tuchman, 1962). On the continent, people waited en masse in Paris to welcome their Cossack defenders. The Germans became concerned as well (Tuchman, 1962). Contemporary reports held that the Kaiser and his senior staff had left France from fear of the “250,000” Russian troops believed to be in the field there, and the German Army was reported to have detached two sorely needed divisions to repel this imaginary invasion from the Steppes.

Readers today may find this account mildly amusing, but essentially irrelevant to our modern lives. The First World War seems lost in remote antiquity, with the Red Baron, perhaps better known today for pizza than for aerial victories, flying about in a powered box-kite, and antique cannons being dragged around mud-soaked battlefields by teams of panicked horses. The whole thing may seem as remote to modern people as Crecy or Agincourt.

But if you were able to examine the brain of a person in 1914, you would find no substantive difference between that brain and the one in the head of any modern Internet-ridden person today. The effects of inaccurate prior frameworks, of stress-related reduction in critical thinking, and of the uncritical sharing of purported eyewitness accounts would be psychologically the same in the worlds of 1914 and 2026.

However, there would be an important exception today, based on our technology rather than our psychology. Unlike the word-of-mouth campaigns that spread false rumors in clubs and at railway stations in 1914, we of 2026 have the internet to spread false rumors worldwide at electronic speeds, either by mistake or by design on the part of people who have something to gain. We also have AI-generated imagery so advanced that its products are virtually impossible for most of us to tell from reality.

The remote and imaginary reports of Russians in Scotland in 1914 are more than a quaint episode in the history of eyewitness memory. They form a significant warning for those of us in the modern age of technology. Today, more than in any previous era, we must be very careful in our assessment of evidence, eyewitness, visual, and otherwise, and very aware of how the principles governing our psychology may influence that assessment.

Bransford, J. D., and Johnson, M. K. 1973. Considerations of Some Problems of Comprehension. In W. G. Chase (Ed.), Visual Information Processing. Orlando, FL: Academic Press.

Pennell, C. 2015. Believing the Unbelievable: The Myth of the Russians with 'Snow On Their Boots' in the United Kingdom, 1914. Cultural and Social History, 11, 69-87.

Sharps, M.J. 2022. Processing Under Pressure: Stress, Memory, and Decision-Making in Law Enforcement (3rd ed.). Park City, Utah: Blue 360 Media.

Sharps, M.J. 2024. The Forensic View: Investigative Psychology, Law Enforcement, Space Aliens, Exploration, and the Nature of Madness. Las Vegas: Amazon.

Sharps, M.J., Herrera, M.R., and Price‐Sharps, J.L. 2013. Situationally Equivocal Eyewitness Evidence and the Violence of Crimes. Journal of Investigative Psychology and Offender Profiling, 10, DOI: 10.1002/jip.1398

Sharps, M.J., & Price-Sharps, J.L. 2026. Dissociation and Belief: The Psychology of Why Things Go Horribly Wrong, and What To Do About It. Las Vegas: Amazon.

Tuchman, B.W. 1962. The Guns of August. New York: Ballantine.

#4638. World War II’s baby gas masks are as unnerving as you’d imagine

Published Oct 30, 2026 9:54 AM EDT

Time forgets the vast majority of inventions—usually for good reason. As parents and children everywhere get ready for trick-or-treating, we’d like to turn your attention to one such invention: the baby gas mask.

In the November 1938 issue of Popular Science, “a doll demonstrates the use of the baby gas mask” in an undeniably creepy image. The word mask is perhaps a misnomer here, because this contraption actually completely engulfs the baby as “filtered air is pumped in with an artificial lung.”

These baby gas masks were developed at a time when around the world people feared another world war would—and eventually did—ignite. The brief story on the contraption reads, “Babies are protected from poison gas in case of a wartime attack” by these novel masks.

But it’s still hard to imagine any baby well-behaved enough to sit inside such a creepy invention. Nonetheless, the French inventors behind the technology thought this would be a good idea—even a profitable one. And in the lead up to World War II, the baby gas mask briefly caught on, with several vintage photographs showing off different iterations of the device.

In one 1937 image (featured above), a woman and young toddler both sport gas masks in Germany.

There’s also a whole slew of children and babies wearing gas masks in vintage photographs from England. One photograph (below) shows how a baby gas mask, also known as a hood, worked as a woman demonstrates using the contraption at the historic Holborn Town Hall in London, England.

This particular design took three years to develop. An infant is placed inside a fabric hood featuring a large cellulose acetate window. A drawstring cinches the hood at the infant’s waist, so that the arms, shoulders, and head are completely contained. An adult then operates a rubber bellows to filter air into the hood.

There was apparently no time limit for how long a child could be kept inside the airtight mask—as long as air was steadily pumped in, of course. As to whether the infant enjoyed the contraption, no one could ask.

Another photograph taken (fittingly) during Halloween season, on October 20, 1937, at Dr. Barnardo’s nursery home in Hawkhurst, Kent, England, shows several toddlers in a more traditional face gas mask. The home was actually nicknamed the Babies’ Castle. It originally opened in 1883, after a Mr. Theodore Moillet donated two adjacent mansions and an acre of meadowland for the nursery.

Yet another photograph from England shows several mothers holding babies fitted with the hood-style gas mask designed by the Royal Air Force.

Hospitals in England were also fitted with baby gas masks, and one 1940 photograph shows several nurses testing out the new technology.

One little girl named Jean Panter even convinced her father to make her doll a gas mask. This photograph of little Jean with her doll was taken in England on February 11, 1938, shortly before World War II began. The fact that even a young girl wanted a gas mask for her beloved toy certainly speaks to how much fears of poison gas permeated society before and during World War II.

In 1938, Dr. Jacques Marie Le Mée (sometimes spelled La Mee or Le-Mee), the head physician at the Hôpital Necker-Enfants-Malades in Paris, developed another type of baby gas mask. In fact, the hospital Le Mée worked at is the oldest children’s hospital in the Western world, initially founded in 1801 as Hôpital des Enfants Malades.

In one 1939 photograph, several women and their babies don Le Mée’s baby gas mask in a Parisian square. As opposed to the baby gas hoods on display in vintage English photographs, Le Mée’s invention envelopes the entire baby’s body. Even the baby’s legs will get clean air.

Even though the November 1938 issue of Popular Science says the baby gas mask gracing its pages was developed in France, it’s markedly different to the above photograph of Le Mée’s baby gas mask.

In this design, the window is larger and it’s also unclear how the baby gas mask cinches or becomes airtight around the infant.

Someone holding the child pumps fresh air into the hood-style gas mask. “The person holding the infant controls the amount of fresh air entering the [baby] shelter by pressing on the rubber-lung unit,” the short story in the magazine reads.

But even in dark times, children always find a way to have fun. In one delightful comment on a BBC story about baby gas masks, one reader, William Irwin, remembers having “endless fun playing ‘divers’ with one” baby gas mask.

“We were so far removed from bombing risk areas so I do not believe I was ever put into it as a war-baby. It gave me the interest to eventually become a scuba sports diver.”

Even though this technology thankfully fell by the wayside and seems very strange to modern eyes, it still offers us a lot to think about. The inventions that come out of hard times can even inspire—at least if you’re William Irwin.

In That Time When, Popular Science tells the weirdest, most surprising, and little-known stories that shaped science, engineering, and innovation.

#4637. Seven young condors released in northern California

Published Oct 30, 2026 11:12 AM EDT

In 1986, there wasn’t a single California condor (Gymnogyps californianus) left in the wild. Thankfully, it wasn’t because the birds of prey had gone extinct, but they were getting close. In the 1980s, there were fewer than two dozen condors remaining in the wild. That’s why the United States Fish and Wildlife Service moved them into a captive breeding and release program.

Now, the Northern California Condor Restoration Program has released seven young condors into the wild in Yurok Country, close to the Oregon border, according to a statement emailed to Popular Science. One of the birds is particularly special—the condor represents the 200th California condor hatched at the San Diego Zoo Safari Park to be released into the wild. In total, the safari park has hatched 291 condors since 1982.

The seven recently released condors will join 26 other condors already enjoying the Yurok Country site. It’s the most recently established California condor release site, and received its first released condors in 2022. The NCCRP is a collaboration between the Yurok Tribe and the Redwood National and State Parks.

“Condor releases are critical to achieving our ultimate goal- to reestablish a self-sustaining condor population in the wild,” Joe Burnett, California Condor Recovery Program Manager at the Ventana Wildlife Society in California, previously told Popular Science.

It was Burnett that taught us about an unexpected behavior in young condors: the “zoomies” we more frequently associate with dogs.

“We observe the zoomies in both captive and wild condors. It’s just a sudden expression of pure excitement for young condors and very fun to watch,” Burnett explained at the time. “They just can’t contain themselves and totally let loose. They hop, run in circles, or flap around, or all the above! It’s just pure fun!”

It’s unclear whether the special “200th” bird experienced such a display. Either way, the release is happy news. There are now seven more condors in the wild, when only a few years ago there were none.

#4636. XCMG debuts new, fully autonomous electric terminal tractor [video]

The new XCMG SDA411 concept terminal truck is fully electric, has no cabin, and an L4 autonomous tech stack that’s purpose-built for unmanned logistics – and, if XCMG get their way, it looks like the future of drayage truck operations.

Whether you call them terminal trucks, yard dogs, or anything else, these heavy-duty trucks do work that’s ideally suited to electrification. It’s all low-speed, high-torque, short distance, precision operation, all the time. And the quiet, vibration-free, instant power operation of electric drive is in its element.

Chinese equipment brand XCMG gets it, and they’re taking the electric terminal truck concept a step further with the debut of an all-new, cab-less design that’s 100% autonomous.

“With no cab and an L4 autonomous driving system, the platform is purpose-built for unmanned logistics,” said XCMG, on LinkedIn. “Its 360° perception system enables autonomous navigation, obstacle avoidance, task execution and parking, supporting continuous mixed-traffic operations in demanding environments.”

That same post included a video showing the SDA411 make its way around XCMG’s campus, making some emergency stops, and pulling up to a charger for a human attendant to plug it in (I guess they haven’t heard about Fortescue’s trick with the KUKA welding robot, yet). You can check out the post for yourself, below.

As for the autonomous aspect, while I generally side with labor and humanity over management and technology, there’s some truth to the industry claims that young people don’t want to drive trucks anymore, even with the promise of six-figure salaries.

Combine that with an aging workforce and not enough new talent entering the field, and virtually every industrial sector is struggling with a serious operator shortage. Autonomous equipment like the SDA411 could help address that shortage, keeping goods moving even when there aren’t enough drivers to go around. And rather than simply replacing workers, the technology could let experienced operators oversee multiple vehicles, take on supervisory roles and stay in the industry longer, while making these jobs accessible to people who might not otherwise be able to do them.

It doesn’t have to be autonomous because it’s electric it only needs to be powered by electric motors not gas to be better in every way.

If XCMG get their way, we’ll get to see how that all plays out somewhat sooner than later. In the meantime, we’ll have to settle for hearing what you think about the SDA411 and how it could impact brands like Kalmar and Orange EV in the comments.

#4635. Male black bear ‘Nugget’ wins Introvert Award for his adorable hiding technique

Published Oct 30, 2026 11:48 AM EDT

Like the patient Paul, a male black bear (Ursus americanus) named Nugget would rather hang back alone than jump right into the salmon fest. For his solo tendencies, the team at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska have awarded Nugget the 2026 Introvert Award.

“For much of the season, Nugget could be seen wedged between rocks by lower falls,” the U.S. Forest Service team writes. “If you saw a furry, black head with glassy eyes poking out of a crack—that’s Nugget! You could also find him perched on a rock waiting for his turn to fish in the lower falls hierarchy; afraid to assert his dominance in the crowd.”

Nugget was first spotted in the area only two years ago, and is beloved for his small size. He has a reddish coat that shifts to black later in the season. Nugget is often described as “scrappy.” He mostly scavenged during his first season at the creek, but slowly learned to catch salmon.

“The pristine ecosystem around Anan Creek allows even small, scrappy bears like Nugget to thrive,” the Rangers write.

The U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest are currently doling out the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory over the summer.

The nation’s largest national forest, Tongass covers most of Southeast Alaska, including the capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 known bears feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Like their chunky counterparts further north in Katmai National Park, the bears return annually each summer to eat salmon and teach their young how to fish and survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear and explore.org’s cameras also broadcast live streams of their antics.

#4634. Why We Delay Important Decisions

We’re all holding onto something we’re sure we can’t give up on, but research shows that letting go can boost our happiness a lot more than we might think.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

I’m sure you can relate to putting off an important decision until next week, then the week after that, and then the week after that. Maybe you need to decide where you would like to relocate, choose a healthcare provider, or determine whether to move forward with an important medical procedure. You know the decision needs your attention, but you keep finding reasons to wait.

Most of us may think of procrastination as putting things off because we are busy or lack motivation. However, what if we are not avoiding the task itself, but the uncertainty that comes with making a decision? Oftentimes, the most difficult part is not knowing what to do, but accepting that we cannot predict how things will turn out.

Experts argue that one reason this happens is negative reinforcement. When avoiding something uncomfortable brings relief, our brains will likely desire to avoid it again. Consider, for example, when a deadline gets pushed back. In the moment, you may feel better knowing you have more time to complete the task at hand, even though you know that the work still needs to get done. Delaying an important decision can have the same effect. We may receive temporary relief, however the decision still remains unresolved.

In my work with people facing difficult life decisions, I have seen how the desire to avoid making the wrong choice can become a significant barrier. People may spend considerable time weighing possibilities, seeking reassurance, and revisiting the same concerns.

Another reason important decisions can be difficult to make is that we want to make the best possible choice. Experts describe this tendency as maximizing. It involves searching for the best available option, rather than choosing one that meets our needs and priorities. Wanting to make a good decision is reasonable, but constantly searching for something better can make it harder to settle on an option.

Let's think about someone deciding whether to relocate for a new job. The opportunity they are considering may offer better pay and career growth, however accepting it could mean leaving family, familiar surroundings, and comfort. They may continue comparing options and questioning whether another opportunity would have been better, even after obtaining enough information to inform their decision.

Recent research offers some insight into this pattern. For instance, in a 2024 study, researchers examined how people with maximizing tendencies estimate the time they spend making decisions. Results showed that "maximizers" tended to underestimate how much time they spent comparing and reconsidering their options. They likely don't realize they are making decision-making harder not easier for themselves.

Making a decision becomes even more challenging when we are faced with too many options to select from. For instance, someone who has decided to undergo a medical procedure, but must choose how to pay for it, has to decide on using a credit card, applying for a medical credit line, choosing an in-house payment plan, or financing through a third-party company, which adds another decision to an already important one.

One emerging example in the healthcare industry is "first-look financing." An article by Cherry describes how this concept introduces one preferred financing option first while keeping other options available. This approach reflects choice architecture, which examines how the presentation of choices can influence people's decisions.

For example, after a patient agrees to move forward with a medical procedure, the clinic might first explain its preferred third-party financing option, including the monthly payment and application process. If the patient is not comfortable with that option, the provider can then discuss other options, such as an in-house payment plan or using a credit card.

Here are a few ways to make important decisions feel more manageable:

Putting off important decisions is something many of us experience, especially when we are uncertain about what may happen next. Avoiding a decision can make us feel better temporarily, but it does not necessarily make the situation easier. Ultimately, we do not have to find the perfect option or know exactly how everything will turn out before moving forward. Sometimes, making a good-enough decision and taking one small step at a time is what can help us move past the uncertainty.

Cheek, N. N., & Schwartz, B. (2016). On the meaning and measurement of maximization. Judgment and Decision Making, 11(2), 126–146. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1930297500007257

Huang and Li (2024). “How Maximizers Estimate Their Decision Time: The Mediating Effect of Memory Reduction.” Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 37(3).

#4633. Amflow launches two powerful new electric bikes, including its first SUV-style e-bike

Amflow, the electric bicycle brand that burst onto the scene with some of the most powerful and lightweight electric mountain bikes on the market, is expanding its lineup with two major releases. The company has announced global availability of its new Amflow TL Carbon, while also bringing its removable-battery Amflow PR Carbon series to the US for the first time.

Both models are powered by the latest Avinox mid-drive motor systems, which have quickly earned a reputation for delivering impressive power in surprisingly compact packages.

The biggest departure from Amflow’s roots is the new TL Carbon, which takes the company’s high-performance mountain biking DNA and applies it to a more versatile SUV-style electric bike. While less common in the US (ironically), SUV-style e-bikes are essentially a hybrid electric bicycle designed to act as an all-in-one, “do-it-all” vehicle combining the rugged build and off-road capability of an electric mountain bike with the practical, everyday utility of a city or trekking bike.

Rather than focusing exclusively on technical trails and aggressive mountain biking, the TL Carbon is designed to handle everything from daily commuting to touring and off-road adventures. And with Avinox’s RS800 battery featuring 800Wh of capacity, it’s got plenty of energy on board for diverse adventures.

The full-suspension bike uses the Avinox M2 motor, delivering up to 125 Nm of torque, which should provide more than enough grunt for steep climbs, heavy loads, and just about anything else riders can throw at it.

Avinox e-bike drive systems are known for many things, but chief among them is the extremely high power and torque they offer, eclipsing most other mid-drive motor systems on the market.

Despite that power and versatility, the TL Carbon weighs as little as 22.6 kg (49.8 lb). It also boasts an impressive maximum total weight capacity of 200 kg (441 lb), including the bike itself, rider, and cargo carried on its front and rear racks.

That’s a compelling combination for riders who want the performance of a premium electric mountain bike but need something practical enough to replace a car for everyday trips.

And perhaps most surprisingly, the price isn’t completely outrageous. The Amflow TL Carbon starts at $3,899 in the US and €3,499 in Germany, positioning it competitively against premium European trekking and SUV-style e-bikes.

Meanwhile, American riders are finally getting access to the Amflow PR Carbon series, which had previously launched in other markets.

Unlike Amflow’s earlier electric mountain bikes, the PR series features a removable battery, addressing one of the biggest practical complaints about high-performance eMTBs with integrated batteries.

The new 800 Wh battery weighs just 4 kg (8.8 lb) and can be removed for convenient indoor charging or swapped for a fresh battery to extend a ride. That’s especially useful for riders who don’t have a convenient charging outlet near their bike storage area.

Amflow claims up to 158 km (98 miles) of range under ideal conditions, though that’s based on relatively gentle riding on flat pavement in Eco mode. Riders tackling technical trails with high assistance levels should expect considerably less. But any way you slice it, 800 Wh is a huge battery for eMTBs and should deliver plenty of range under most conditions.

The standard PR Carbon uses the Avinox M2 motor with up to 125 Nm of torque, while the higher-end PR Carbon Pro upgrades to the more powerful Avinox M2S motor, producing up to 150 Nm of torque.

In the US, the PR Carbon starts at $4,999, while the PR Carbon Pro commands $6,799. European pricing starts at €4,499 and €5,899, respectively, based on German pricing.

All three bikes are available beginning today through ⁠Amflow’s official website and its network of authorized dealers. In the US, both models generally arrive as Class 1 e-bikes (no throttle) with a top speed of 20 mph (32 km/h), though Amflow models can typically be unlocked to Class 3 performance with a top speed of 28 mph (45 km/h).

Amflow has been one of the more interesting brands to watch in the premium e-bike space, largely because of how aggressively it has pushed the boundaries of motor performance and bike weight.

But these latest releases show that the company is thinking beyond simply building increasingly powerful electric mountain bikes.

The TL Carbon is particularly interesting to me because it brings that impressive Avinox performance to a more practical platform. As someone who spends a minority of my riding time in the dirt, Amflow suddenly looks a lot more interesting to me, personally. Not everyone needs a dedicated eMTB, but plenty of riders would appreciate a lightweight, powerful, well-equipped electric bike that can handle both weekday commuting and weekend adventures.

And the PR Carbon’s removable battery is a welcome development, especially as the industry continues to recognize that convenience and serviceability matter just as much as outright performance.

With the Avinox ecosystem continuing to expand across more bike brands and categories, Amflow is also facing increasing competition from other manufacturers using the same impressive motors. That makes it all the more important for the brand to differentiate itself through thoughtful bike design, not just headline-grabbing power figures.

#4632. World’s tallest Day of the Dead sculpture erected in Mexico City

Published Oct 30, 2026 12:30 PM EDT

Mexico City has broken a Guinness World Record during its preparations for this year’s Day of the Dead (Día de los Muertos) celebrations. At nearly 110 feet tall, the colorful sculpture of a female skeleton currently standing in the capital city’s town square (the Zócalo) is officially the world’s tallest La Catrina monument. The roughly 11-story project made from steel and fiberglass required about 140 people to assemble, and overshadows the town of Puerto Vallarta’s 92.3-foot Catrina built back in 2023. The height isn’t the only impressive aspect, either. Her purple dress measures over 88 feet long, while the memorial altar (called an ofrenda) is surrounded by an estimated 70,00 marigold plants grown in the nearby Xochimilco borough.

Observed each year on November 1 and 2, Mexico’s Day of the Dead is famously dedicated to celebrating and honoring deceased family members and loved ones. Historians are divided on its exact origins—while some researchers contend it possesses genuine Indigenous pre-Hispanic roots, others argue the holiday is a more recent rebrand of Spanish traditions intended to promote cultural pride. Regardless of the answer, Day of the Dead has evolved into one of the country’s most popular and iconic observances. Every year, celebrants often wear skeleton-themed costumes and construct ofrendas, while families and friends gather to fondly recall the departed.

Apart from its size, Mexico City’s record-breaking sculpture is a relatively traditional example of La Catrina, one of Day of the Dead’s most recognizable figures. It’s also much easier to trace La Catrina’s history compared to the holiday’s origins. The figure is based on early 20th century Mexican illustrator José Guadalupe Posada’s most famous work, “La Calavera Catrina” ( or “The Elegant Skull”). Posada’s illustration was released posthumously, and depicts a woman’s skeleton dressed in stylish clothing. Art historians widely view “La Calavera Catrina” as a critique of upper-class Mexican women who attempted to mirror European fashions of the era. Posada’s piece was later expanded upon by the muralist Diego Rivera in 1946-1947.

Similarly inspired iconography has since become a mainstay of Day of the Dead celebrations. La Catrina sculptures like the new record breaker in Mexico City are frequently surrounded by marigolds. Also known as cempasúchil, the flowers are traditionally believed to help guide spirits home with their scent and colorful petals.

Like life itself, Mexico City’s building-sized La Catrina is only temporary. Admirers will be able to visit the installation and its altar only until November 2.
