#4631. All aboard! Massachusetts is getting 10 new electric transit trains

The Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) board of directors voted unanimously Thursday to approve the purchase of a new generation of battery-powered public transit trains – and they can’t arrive soon enough.

“(MBTA) has, obviously, an immediate need for locomotives,” explains William Wolfgang, the MBTA’s senior director of vehicle engineering. The new machines will replace the oldest locomotives in the MBTA fleet, GP40s built more than 50 years ago and F40s that are well over 30 years old. In a presentation to the MTBA board, MTBA said 13 of the GP40s have, “exceeded their useful life,” while the F40s will reach the end of their life between 2029 and 2035.

The MBTA will put in an order for 20 Siemens-built “Charger” locomotives; 10 Tier 4 diesel-powered hybrid electric units and 10 dual-mode battery/catenary electric units – and, beyond trackside power for charging the batteries, there are other challenges presented by going electric, most notably using existing cab cars to control the battery-electric units. “We’re going to have to work with railroad operations, engineering, and the Brotherhood of [Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen] to try and determine the best way to handle that,” adds Wolfgang. “That will be an upcoming change order once we get into the design review process.”

The total bill comes out to $310.4 million. A combination of state and federal funding will pay for the order, including a recent $200 million transfer from the Massachusetts Department of Transportation.

The contract includes an option for additional locomotives, although details were not discussed during the meeting. Delivery of the new Siemens Charger trains is set to begin in 2029, with all 20 set to be in service by the end of 2030. Siemens has delivered 440 Charger model hybrid- and battery-electric locomotives globally at the time of this writing.

#4630. In 1841, flesh and blood rained down in Tennessee

Published Oct 30, 2026 1:53 PM EDT

One August day in 1841, near Lebanon, Tennessee, two enslaved people heard the sound of rain pattering on the tobacco leaves around them. But this was no ordinary rain: It was a deep red color. The sky, it seemed, was raining blood. Even more alarming, small pieces of flesh and fat seemed to be raining down, too. The two witnesses took the leaves inside to show their enslaver, Mr. E.M. Chandler, who quickly reported the event to his neighbors.

In an attempt to clear things up, pieces of fallen material were sent to Dr. Gerard Troost, a renowned scientist and collector of natural history specimens. Upon opening the package, Troost noted that it “had the offensive smell of putrid animal matter.” After a thorough analysis, Dr. Troost’s assessment was clear: “There is no doubt but that this substance is animal matter and belongs to our globe.”

The flesh and blood fall near Lebanon in 1841 was far from the only time blood rain or flesh has fallen from the sky, nor was it the last. Both experts and lay people have put forward various explanations for blood rains and flesh falls, including animals being torn up by storms, hoaxes, carcasses dropped by vultures, meteor dust, algal spores, or even red discharge from butterflies.

The 1841 blood rain incident in Lebanon has to be contextualized within the buildup to the Civil War, and a massacre that happened almost exactly 10 years earlier. In 1831, an enslaved carpenter and preacher named Nat Turner in Southampton, Virginia began having visions of “lights in the sky to which the children of darkness gave other names than what they really were—for they were the lights of the Saviour’s hands,” followed by sightings of “drops of blood on the corn, as though it were dew from heaven.”

When Turner later found hieroglyphic marks written in blood on leaves in the woods, he took it as an omen: Shortly afterwards, he led one of the deadliest uprisings of enslaved people in U.S. history. From August 21 to August 23, 1831, Nat Turner and his followers killed 55 white people. In response, local militias and roving mobs killed an unknown number of both enslaved and free Black people. Nat Turner and some of his followers were sentenced to death and executed.

When enslaved people discovered blood on the tobacco leaves in Lebanon in 1841, the fuss was enormous, and echoed Nat Turner’s accounts of bloody rain. Locals in Lebanon wrote about their local blood rain incident in letters to relatives, newspapers from near and far reported on it, and the farm became somewhat of a circus.

A visitor from another town, William F. Cooper, wrote in his journal that “the smell of this fallen matter was very offensive, polluting the whole air.” Cooper also described the extent of the fall as “from 40 to 60 yards in width, and six or eight hundred yards in length,” equivalent to around six to eight football fields.

After Dr. Troost later analyzed the material and determined it was, in fact, animal matter, the flesh fall was reported in the American Journal of Science. Troost’s primary theory was that a strong wind “might have taken up part of an animal which was in a state of decomposition, and have brought it in contact with an electric cloud, in which it was kept in a state of partial fluidity or viscosity.”

After the Lebanon flesh and blood fall, stories of Nat Turner and the slave rebellion were revived in full force. Many white Southerners feared another uprising. On the other hand, Northerners saw the blood rain as a heavenly critique on the practice of slavery.

On September 10, 1841, The Wisconsin Enquirer reported that residents in Northern states had likened the Lebanon event to the blood fall in Virginia that occurred before Nat Turner’s uprising, and “construed the mysterious shower [in Lebanon] into a judgment from heaven, designed to warn the slave-holding states of the iniquity of their traffic in flesh and blood.”

The mystery of the flesh and blood fall in Lebanon was never totally resolved, and was eventually dismissed as a hoax perpetrated by the two enslaved people who witnessed it first. This was later rebutted in The Western Journal of Medicine and Surgery in December 1841.

“People have a need for an explanation, just any explanation, regardless of whether or not it is the explanation,” says Tom Maxwell, writer, blood rain researcher, and host of The Night Parade podcast. “In this case, I think culturally a lot of people needed it to be a hoax.”

Blood rains and flesh falls stretch far back into history. They are mentioned in both The Iliad and the Bible. Philosophers, scientists, and storytellers have described numerous incidents throughout the centuries, including in ancient Rome, medieval Ireland, the 19th century United States, and around the world today.

Nineteenth-century scientists even attempted to find a scientific reason for these falls with microscopes. These scientists could determine “it was always blood. It was always animal material,” says Maxwell. “The question was how did it get where it got, not what it was.” Contemporary scientists have narrowed in on these two separate questions: First, what is falling from the sky, and second, how did it get in the sky?

While blood rains and flesh falls are often discussed together, there are likely different mechanisms behind them. One common explanation for flesh falls lines up with what Troost proposed in 1841: a strong storm, or even vultures, can sweep flesh up into the sky and drop it down later. Strange weather events like this are not unheard of, and fish falls, insect tornadoes, or even frogs falling from the sky have all been documented before.

Blood rain, on the other hand, has a completely different explanation. In these cases, the rain is red because it likely contains dust or microorganisms rather than animal matter. This was hard to detect in the past.

“They didn’t have the science,” says Dr. Patrick McCafferty, a researcher at Chemnitz University of Technology who has studied how myths and literature often record real-world comets, meteor strikes, or other catastrophes. “So [from their perspective] this seems to be something sent by God to punish them.”

The reality is that since Christians were largely familiar with the concept of an impending doomsday and blood rain in the Bible, “They would interpret these things as blood,” says McCafferty. “They’re also primed to look out for these signs of the end of the world.”

Bloody rains studied in the past few decades have given clues as to what the substance may be, at least in some cases. One key example of this is the blood rain that fell in Kerala, India, in 2001.

Researchers collected samples of the red rain, and found it contained algal or seaweed spores, which caused the red coloration. Another research group argued the Kerala blood rain was the result of dust blown over from desert areas in West Asia.

Yet another group asserted that the Kerala blood rain was red because it was full of “bacteria-like material that had been swept to Earth from a passing comet.” They argued that if a comet had broken apart in the Earth’s atmosphere, extraterrestrial particles could have made it into the clouds, raining down as blood-red droplets.

Despite the frequent co-occurrence of meteors or comets and blood rain (a route of investigation also pursued by McCafferty) the explanation has not been widely adopted.

With so many eyewitness accounts of blood rains and flesh falls across the centuries, it’s hard to dismiss the phenomenon. “Chances are, it was real. Chances are, it was caused by something,” says McCafferty. “I’m conscious that things happen that do not have a good explanation.”

When it comes to meat, fat, or red rain falling from the sky, we shouldn’t be too quick to dismiss what it really looks like: flesh and blood. “The classic example is the [French Academy of Sciences] completely dismissing accounts that stones fell from the sky,” says McCafferty.

“So when anybody would come to them with a meteorite, they would say ‘This was hit by thunder or this was hit by lightning. This is a thunderstone. It was hit by lightning. It did not fall from space. It’s stupid to believe stones fall from space.’ And then it turns out that, oh, actually they do.”

Many questions about blood rain and flesh falls remain unanswered. In Maxwell’s opinion, that’s okay: “In the face of the inexplicable,” he says, “I think the most appropriate epistemological response is ‘I don’t know.’”

#4629. Send your name to Saturn’s largest moon

Published Oct 30, 2026 2:34 PM EDT

NASA is still on track to send its Dragonfly rotocraft to Saturn’s moon Titan by the end of the decade, and you can come along for the ride. Well, you can at least add your initials to the flight roster.

As part of its Journey to Titan campaign, NASA has opened an online registry that will be included on a microchip aboard the spacecraft when it launches. The launch is currently scheduled for no earlier than July 2028. Signees will receive a personalized digital “boarding pass,” as proof that their names will reach the ice-encased Saturnian moon in 2034. While the encoded autographs may not do much to help with the overall mission, it’s nice to know that you will be represented on what may become one of the most consequential space endeavors of all time.

“We are excited to bring humanity along for the journey of a lifetime, and we invite everyone to send their names on this small, but mighty rotorcraft that will unlock the secrets of the universe,” Nicky Fox, NASA’s Science Mission Directorate associate administrator, said in the announcement.

Titan is the largest of Saturn’s 292 known moons, and a longtime dream destination in the search for life beyond Earth. Although Titan features dusty dunes overlooking lakes and rivers of methane, the frigid surface also maintains a temperature of around −290 degrees Fahrenheit. This is inhospitable to life as we know it, but a giant ocean also exists beneath the icy shell. Astrobiologists widely agree that these waters probably contain enough complex compounds to facilitate a prebiotic environment. Laboratory simulations of Titan’s atmosphere have also indicated its gaseous conditions can even form some of the principle building blocks for DNA and RNA. If true, extraterrestrial microbial life may exist within the moon’s hidden waters.

However, there’s no way to confirm the possibility without directly examining Titan’s conditions. That’s where Dragonfly comes into play. After over six years of interplanetary travel, NASA’s eight-bladed robotic rotocraft will land on the moon and begin its environmental survey. Dragonfly’s vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) capabilities will allow it to travel to multiple locations over the planned three-year mission. If all goes well, the rotocraft will journey across 70 miles on Titan, while visiting 20 to 30 different areas.

“By flying the first-ever rotorcraft science mission, NASA will…we search for signs of habitability on a distant world that is most similar to our own,” added Fox.

Dragonfly is currently under construction at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland. It marks the fourth mission in NASA’s New Frontiers Program, which is dedicated to further exploration of the planets and moons that comprise our solar system.

Adding your name to Dragonfly’s log is likely a no-brainer for many people, but there is no rush if you need to take some time to ponder the decision. Signees have until 11:59 p.m. EST on January 15, 2027, to make their (digital) mark.

#4628. Range Energy shows how its eTrailer saves almost as much as a Tesla Semi

Range Energy, a company working to electrify trucking through the use of a trailer with its own battery and motors, has published an analysis showing how much fleets can save through electrification – and just at the right time, with diesel at record highs.

You may have heard a little something about diesel prices lately, which have just about doubled in less than a year due to Donald Trump’s war of choice in Iran.

Diesel is now at record highs, and it’s devastating fleets and truck drivers and anyone who uses any products that are delivered on trucks (so, everyone). It’s an urgent problem that needs an urgent solution, and solutions are not forthcoming from the responsible entities.

So, fleets have to seek another solution, and Range Energy would like to be the one that provides it.

Range is a startup based in California, founded and staffed by former Tesla employees and others from around the EV industry. It’s building an electrified trailer which we demoed at ACT Expo in 2024 (really, watch it, it’s a very cool demo) which promises to cut fleet fuel use significantly.

It does this by having its own battery and motors inside the trailer, meaning the tractor doesn’t have to work nearly as hard as the trailer can effectively pull its own weight. Even though the tractor still runs on diesel, it uses a whole lot less of it.

This differs from the other popular option for fleets: full electrification. There are a number of electric semi tractors available, and fleets have been moving to install them, getting their depots ready for charging. But Range lets you bring your own tractor, and electrifies the trailer instead.

Range previously published some early findings, showing a 36% reduction in fuel use in a testing scenario. It also did a pilot program with an egg farm in California, which improved the fuel efficiency of the farm’s diesel fleet by 50-70%.

Now Range has published its own white paper showing comparative savings that fleets can achieve with either its own solution, the eTrailer, or Tesla’s solution, the fully electric Tesla Semi. The paper does not cover the various other electric semi tractors available on the market today, just a face-off between Range and Tesla.

The analysis goes through several scenarios, mostly focusing on refrigerated trailer units (“reefers”), which is the first product Range is focusing on.

Trailer electrification is a great idea for reefers, because they usually fill up on volume rather than weight (called “cubing out”), meaning battery weight doesn’t eat into maximum trailer payload. Batteries also offer power to run refrigeration, meaning you don’t need to have a diesel generator on the trailer.

The upshot of the whole thing is that: fleets can save money with the Range eTrailer, and can theoretically save more money with the Tesla Semi, but the numbers are relatively close in the most common scenario, and the Tesla scenarios have a much wider spread depending on what implementation you consider.

For example, if you only use public chargers rather than your own depot, the Tesla Semi will be more costly because energy will be more expensive to your fleet than if you bought it at commercial utility rates. So, even though installing chargers in your depot sounds expensive, it will pencil out better in the end.

The best money savings came from having two Semis share the same charger, but that requires tight timings and overnight driving.

Another important feature Range points out is build time for a project. The nice thing about the eTrailer is it can slot into fleets immediately with little operational change required, whereas the larger charging needs of an electric tractor) tend to require bigger projects to get a depot ready with chargers (but despite the higher upfront costs, you get better long-term savings, since you avoid diesel entirely with an electric tractor).

In the end, Range found that its solution saves a little more money than the Tesla Semi does in most scenarios, but the difference is quite narrow, with each option having its strengths and weaknesses. Both solutions are better than diesel in most scenarios, but not all of them.

You don’t necessarily need to choose between the two, as an electrified trailer can still be used with an electric tractor. It works the same way in either case – using its own motors to take some of the effort off the tractor. This means extended range, for longer hauls with light loads that couldn’t quite make it on the Tesla Semi’s inherent range. And the benefit of being able to run the reefer while disconnected from the tractor or shore power remains as well.

The analysis has plenty of limitations. It has to estimate future diesel costs (it used a number below current prices, but still historically high), didn’t cover financing costs, it doesn’t have real-world data for the Tesla Semi, didn’t cover electrified tractor or trailer options from other companies, can’t analyze individual charging costs site-to-site since each is specific to a utility company, didn’t cover the myriad incentives available in various regions, and most of all it didn’t consider diesel emissions, which are a huge societal cost to everyone that electrification reduces (and full electrification reduces more).

So in the end, every fleet has a different use case, and should run the numbers themselves to see how either solution would fit in. But in the generalized case, it looks like there are plenty of savings available out there, whether through tractor or trailer electrification.

A good idea in theory but there are three trailers for every tractor-cab because trailers spend a lot of time sitting idle. For specific closed-loop customers and routes this can very very helpful but not as a general solution.

You know what can offer relief right now? Importing Class 8 Trucks. China is selling 280,000 heavy duty EV trucks this year. Trade barriers hurt economies.

Unfortunately, given diesel prices are at record highs right now, both of the options in the paper are a little suboptimal. Tesla Semis have been on order for almost ten years now, and Tesla only just claimed it has started production in earnest. And Range is still about a year out from volume production of its eTrailer, which it says will start in late 2027 – so, while an eTrailer will be able to slot into a fleet immediately when it’s available, it’s not available yet, which puts a damper on that potential benefit.

So neither can offer immediate relief, but both offer good options for fleets to plan for the next inevitable oil shock – which is why Range didn’t base its analysis solely on current prices (remember, we just had another shock in 2022, this nonsense happens all the time, maybe it’s time to stop using oil). But, the numbers in the paper for the Tesla Semi can be compared to numbers for other electric tractors already available today, which can in turn be compared to the costs of the eTrailer, for fleets so inclined to make that comparison.

#4625. Volkswagen gets L3 autonomous driving test permit in China, eyes 2027

Volkswagen Group China now has a permit to test Level 3 autonomous driving on public roads in Hefei, and it says testing is already underway. The permit also covers large-scale driving data collection in the city.

It’s the latest step toward VW’s goal of L3 technology readiness in China by 2027. And the timing is good as the group holds its first China Technology Day in Hefei on Wednesday.

VW says the permit was issued under China’s strictest L3 framework and that its setup meets the country’s latest mandatory safety design standards. It didn’t say which authority issued it, how many vehicles are in the fleet, or which roads they can use.

Hefei makes sense as a base. It’s home to the Volkswagen China Technology Company (VCTC), the group’s largest R&D center outside Germany, and to its Volkswagen Anhui production site.

The software comes from CARIZON, VW’s intelligent driving unit in China, which started as a joint venture between CARIAD and Horizon Robotics. Its driver assistance system is called Hyper Sense 8 (HS8), which VW describes as its first “full-scenario” ADAS.

Behind it is GAIA 2.0, a world model VW built itself. VW says it runs simulation equal to 5 million km of safety testing per day, using about 30 million real-road scenario clips, and it wants to get that to 10 million km per day. VW is also developing its own system-on-chip, the C7H, which it says can support up to Level 4.

Ralf Brandstätter, chairman and CEO of Volkswagen Group China, kept the message on safety. He said the group “will never advance technology at the cost of safety” and called the permit an important step on the road to L3 readiness (our translation from Chinese).

This is a road test permit. VW can’t sell L3 cars to customers with it.

China’s MIIT granted the country’s first L3 product approvals in December 2025 to two sedans: a Changan model capped at 50 km/h on designated Chongqing expressways, and a BAIC Arcfox model capped at 80 km/h on three Beijing routes. GAC’s Hyptec and XPeng already hold L3 road test permits too. So VW isn’t leading here. It’s catching up to Chinese brands on their home turf.

In July, VW, CARIZON, and Horizon Robotics said they would deepen their partnership, giving CARIZON “white-box” access to Horizon’s AI foundation model, and targeted the start of L3 deliveries in the second half of 2027. VW’s L2++ system is rolling out on seven new NEV models from its Chinese joint ventures this year.

VW also leans on XPeng in China. It bought a roughly 5% stake in XPeng in 2023 and co-developed its China zonal electrical architecture, CEA, with the startup.

Outside China, the only Western automaker with a certified L3 system on sale is Mercedes-Benz, whose Drive Pilot works on approved highways in Germany and in California and Nevada. Mercedes also got approval to test Level 4 driving in Beijing back in 2024. Tesla’s FSD remains a Level 2 system everywhere it’s sold, China included.

L3 is where liability moves. When the system is engaged, the automaker is responsible for the driving, not the person in the seat. That’s why so few companies have shipped it, and why the ones that have keep it on a short leash: specific roads, low speeds, mostly traffic jams.

China has been serious about building a framework for automakers to bring this techonology to market, and through it, we are seeing who is interested in this version of autonomy.

Not everyone is. Many automakers, including Tesla, have been talking about “skipping” level 3 and going straight to level 4.

#4624. Psychedelic nasal spray treats depression with toad-inspired goo

Published Oct 30, 2026 3:45 PM EDT

A powerful psychedelic compound best associated with the Sonoran desert toad (Incilius alvarius) has been recreated in a lab and transformed into a fast-acting nasal spray. A recent clinical trial outlined this week in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) suggests this spray could help people with treatment resistant depression, without the often less pleasant element of psychedelics. In the study, a single squeeze of the spray eased patients’ depressive symptoms with benefits lasting throughout the eight week trial.

Crucially, those long-term benefits (which have also been observed in other psychedelic research) didn’t require enduring an all-day mystical trip. Most patients were cleared for release less than two hours after taking the spray. Thankfully, the approach also eliminates the need to fondle a toxic amphibian. That’s potentially a plus both for patients and overharvested toad populations. The finds come amid a resurgence in new research and investment involving psychedelics, supported in part by evolving political attitudes towards the compounds on federal and state levels.

The nasal spray was developed by biotech firm AtaiBeckley. Its  active ingredient is called mebufotenin, which is also known as 5-MeO-DMT. The compound occurs naturally in several places, but it is most famously associated with the secretions of the Sonoran desert toad. For decades, amateur psychonauts have sought out these meaty North American toads for the prominent glands located on the amphibian’s head and hind legs. Squeezing those glands releases a milky secretion (sometimes inaccuracy referred to as venom), which when dried and then vaporized, produces an intense psychedelic experience. Many people who have smoked it describe a profound sense of oneness or ego dissolution, and some even report the sensation of dying.

Though based on the same compound, the drug in the nasal spray is synthetic and made in a lab. The researchers wanted to see if a controlled, clinical dose of 5-MeO-DMT could deliver some of the compound’s reported therapeutic benefits while keeping the overall treatment brief, especially compared with longer-acting psychedelics like psilocybin. They  limited their study to 193 adults between the ages of 18 to 75 with treatment-resistant depression. The participants, who came from the United States, Europe, and Australia, had each already tried at least two antidepressant treatments without success. By some estimates, around a third of all patients experiencing major depressive disorder also have treatment resistant depression.

Each participant received nasal spray in either a low (.3mg), medium (8mg), or high (12mg) dose. Neither the patient, nor the clinical staff or researchers involved knew which dose was given. The most intense psychedelic effects wore off relatively quickly, regardless of the dose. Clinicians checked on the patients at regular intervals to determine if they were deemed safe enough to leave the clinic. Among participants who received the 8-milligram dose, 85 percent were ready for discharge within two hours, compared with 78 percent of those who received the 12-milligram dose.

However, the therapeutic effects of the spray appeared to persist far longer.  Patients who received the medium or high dose showed significantly greater improvement than the comparison group as early as two days after treatment, and that advantage held through the end of the eight-week study. The team measured depression with a clinical scale measuring from 0 to 60, with  higher scores indicating more severe symptoms. After four weeks, the 12 mg group had dropped an average of 11.1 points on that score. The 8mg group dropped an even higher 12.5 points while the .3mg group dropped 5.5 points. These findings suggest the nasal spray application could provide some of the same therapeutic effects of other scheduled therapies less less need to have healthcare workers monitoring patients for many hours at a time.

“In adults with treatment-resistant depression, single doses of intranasal mebufotenin benzoate were well tolerated and produced rapid, robust, and durable reductions in depressive symptoms,” the study authors write. “Intranasal mebufotenin benzoate may improve treatment access and convenience, requiring a shorter monitoring period and fewer clinic visits compared with psilocybin and esketamine, respectively.”

This experimental nasal spray arrives amid a transitionary period for psychedelic research. State governments have shown more interest in the field in recent years, with Oregon and Colorado each launching their own psilocybin programs. Even Texas, a state traditionally associated with a tough on drugs approach, just committed $50 million to research the powerful psychedelic ibogaine. Signs of movement are occurring at the federal level as well. In April, President Donald Trump signed an executive order aimed at accelerating research and FDA approval of psychedelic-based therapies.

Though it attracted significant attention, the executive order is really more signaling than action. It notably does not lower the bar a therapeutic needs to reach before archived FDA approval.

Still, pharmaceutical companies are clearly taking note. Earlier this year, Eli Lilly, the largest pharmaceutical company in the world, acquired AtariBeckley for $2.8 billion. AtaiBeckley developed the nasal spray used in the recent JAMA study.

BYD opened pre-orders for the new Denza N8, a luxury five-seat electric SUV with a CLTC range of over 1,000 km (621 miles).

“The king of large 5-seater pure electric vehicles,” as BYD’s luxury sub-brand Denza calls it, is now available to pre-order in China.

BYD opened pre-orders for the new Denza N8 on Monday, and the results so far “have been excellent,” according to Li Hui, Denza’s general manager.

The new Denza N8 is “definitely the most anticipated luxury SUV of the year,” Li said. Denza confirmed in August that the new version will use its Blade Battery 2.0 and Flash Charging Technology to deliver “a world-leading 1,003 km pure electric range.”

Although BYD has released several luxury EVs that offer more than 1,000 km of CLTC range, such as the Denza Z9 GT, this is its first electric SUV to break the 1,000 km mark under CLTC conditions.

For context, the plug-in hybrid version the new Denza N8 is replacing offered a combined CLTC range of 1,003 km (623 miles) on a full tank of gas and a full charge.

BYD didn’t reveal pre-order prices, but Li confirmed last week that the Denza N8’s official launch is scheduled for November.

It will go on sale after the new Denza N8L, a slightly longer six-seat version. The N8L is available in two versions: Premium and Flagship. The N8L EV Premium starts at 299,800 RMB, or about $45,000, while the Flagship model is priced from 329,800 RMB ($49,000).

Those who place a reservation with a 2,000 RMB ($200) deposit will receive a 5,000 RMB credit as a limited-time special offer.

Measuring 5,150 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,820 mm high, with a 3,075 mm wheelbase, the Denza N8 EV is slightly longer than the Kia EV9 and Hyundai IONIQ 9.

Inside, the five-seat electric SUV features a massive 30″ infotainment screen that spans nearly the entire passenger-side dashboard, plus a new 43″ (1.1 meter) panoramic head-up display (PHUD) at the bottom of the windshield.

Other premium features include zero gravity seating in all rows, a three-spoke steering wheel, wireless phone chargers, and ambient lighting.

The luxury SUV is equipped with a roof-mounted LiDAR to support BYD’s God’s Eye 5.0 smart driving assistance system. It also features DiSus-A, BYD’s intelligent air suspension system, and rear-wheel drive.

The new Denza N8 EV will be available with a single rear-wheel-drive (RWD) or a tri-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain. The RWD version uses a single motor producing either 320 kW (429 hp) or 370 kW (496 hp).

The tri-motor Denza N8 uses BYD’s e3 platform. The setup includes a 270 kW (362 hp) front motor and two 310 kW (416 hp) rear motors, delivering a combined output of 890 kW (1,193 hp).

Regulatory filings earlier this year revealed it will be available with a 130.15 kWh or 105.79 kWh BYD Blade 2.0 battery, offering CLTC ranges of up to 1,003 km and 800 km, respectively.

BYD will announce prices next month, but given that the Denza N8L starts at 299,800 RMB ($45,000), the standard version will likely be priced below it.

#4619. Tesla turns to car rental platform Turo for Full Self-Driving test drives

Turo will soon let US renters search specifically for Teslas with “Full Self-Driving” (Supervised) turned on, using a direct integration with Tesla to verify each car’s FSD status. The feature goes live on October 28.

For Tesla, it’s a new way to put FSD in front of people who don’t own a Tesla, and a new source of the FSD subscriptions that now count toward Elon Musk’s pay package.

Hosts link their Tesla account to Turo, and the platform pulls the car’s FSD status through Tesla’s API. Eligible listings then show that FSD is active, and guests can filter for it.

Turo says “thousands” of FSD-enabled Teslas are already listed. Not a shocker. The Model 3 and Model Y are the third and fourth most popular vehicles on Turo so far this year, according to the company.

Eligible US hosts can also get a free one-month FSD (Supervised) trial. After that, it’s Tesla’s regular $99 per month subscription, a cost hosts will want to recover through their daily rates. Turo didn’t say whether FSD listings will carry a premium.

Turo CEO Andre Haddad called it an “industry-first integration with Tesla” and said that “most travelers have had limited opportunity to experience driver’s assistance technology, but the demand is clear.”

The “industry-first” part is generous. Tesla has been renting out its own cars with FSD included in Southern California since last year, a program we first spotted in the works back in 2023. The new part is verified FSD on a third-party marketplace with far more cars in far more cities.

Tesla went subscription-only with FSD in February, and since then it has been pushing hard to get people to try it, including a free one-year subscription on new Model 3 and Model Y orders.

There’s a reason for the urgency. Tesla reported 1.74 million “active FSD subscriptions” in Q3, a metric it only started disclosing because Musk’s 2025 CEO Performance Award uses it. One of the award’s milestones is 10 million. At last quarter’s pace, Tesla would need about eight more years to get there.

Turo’s release leans heavily on “self-driving” and “driverless” language. It cites its own research claiming that 55% of Americans are interested in “driverless technology” for travel, rising to 71% among Gen Z, and that over a fifth of interested Americans would be comfortable spending seven or more hours in a self-driving car.

But FSD (Supervised) is not driverless. It’s a level 2 driver assistance system, and the person behind the wheel is responsible at all times. Even Haddad calls it “driver’s assistance technology” in the same release.

Renters will be getting into a car they’ve likely never driven, with a system they’ve likely never used. Turo’s safeguard is to encourage guests to review Tesla’s FSD documentation and safety guidelines before pickup. That’s it.

We saw what over-trust looks like just two weeks ago, when a driver told the CHP he was asleep with FSD engaged before his Tesla hit a patrol car inside a lane closure in Fairfield, California. Two officers were seriously injured.

Turo also didn’t say who’s on the hook when a guest crashes with FSD engaged: the renter, the host, or Turo’s protection plans.

This is basically ‘Tesla network’ but supervised. Since 2016, Elon Musk has been saying that Tesla owners are going to be able to put their vehicles in the ‘Tesla Network’ to provide rides for others and earn income.

This vision has been delayed for years, but the best they can do right now is combining Turo and FSD.

Usually when I rent a Tesla on Turo the owner has turned off all self steering features. So far, they appear to be more confident in my driving than letting FSD do the work. Given the risks of letting a person unfamiliar with your car drive it, I think if they sincerely believed FSD was safer they would have it on all the time and not let me near the steering wheel. This speaks volumes about FSD.

For Tesla, it should be good for FSD adoption. A weekend road trip with FSD is a much better test drive than 15 minutes around the block with a Tesla advisor, and Turo gets a feature no rental company has.

However, I don’t want to be a party pooper, but I do worry about the complacency issue. Turo is pitching “self-driving” to travelers, and Tesla still calls the product “Full Self-Driving” in the US, even after it dropped the name in Europe under pressure from German regulators. Put a tourist who has never used FSD behind the wheel with that framing, and some of them will treat it as a chauffeur. That’s exactly how you end up with a driver asleep at freeway speed.

At a minimum, Turo should require a short in-app FSD walkthrough before a guest can use it, and spell out liability before someone finds out the hard way. Tesla, which collects the subscriptions, should want the same.

#4616. Cybertruck driver stopped in Germany, ‘Monster truck’ not allowed on roads

A Tesla Cybertruck was pulled over while driving in Germany, a reminder that the vehicle is generally not legal on European roads.

The Tesla Cybertruck has attracted plenty of attention, mostly for its unconventional and polarizing look. For better or worse*, the car looks different than anything else on the road, and thus has been the target of all sorts of discussion (*it’s for worse).

But it’s not just the look of the car that’s unconventional. Because of that look, it also breaks several European rules, particularly those related to pedestrian protection (which was called out immediately upon reveal by many observers, including this author).

As a result, it does not have “type approval” in Germany. Even applications for individual exemptions have been denied because of the vehicle “deviates significantly” from requirements.

The vehicle is also too large. In general, a “class B” license, the normal license you get for driving a car, allows you to drive a vehicle up to 3,500kg (7,716lb). The Cybertruck does weigh less than this, but this number refers to the “Gross Vehicle Weight,” or the maximum weight of the truck when laden with occupants and cargo, for which all trims of the Cybertruck exceed 3,500kg.

A Swedish driver ran up against this barrier when driving through Bavaria, near the town of Vaterstatten, Merkur.de reports (with the funny title “Tesla monster truck stopped on A99”). The driver was holding a class B license, like most drivers, whereas the police said that a C1 license allowing operation of a vehicle up to 7.5 tons would be required.

The police did not allow the driver to continue on their journey. Vaterstatten is near the Southern border of Germany, so the Cybertruck might not have been on German roads for long… except the driver is Swedish, so if they drove all the way from Sweden, they would have spent quite a while on German roads before being stopped.

German here: Technically it is possible to register a modified Cybertruck in a European country and drive it legally on European roads. But you can't register it in Germany, you are only allowed to drive it here occasionally and for less than one year. And you still need a truck driver license (typ "C1" for up to 7.5 tonnes) or an older German license "Führerscheinklasse 3", and it has to be limited to max 90 km/h (approx 56 mph).

This guy from Sweden has somehow managed to register it in Poland. Still the car was not limited in top speed and he didn't have the necessary license for more than 3,5 t maximum weight. So he wasn't allowed to drive any further and probably had to pay high fines.

We’ve seen similar situations before in Europe, with an imported Cybertruck being seized in the UK, someone trying to smuggle two through Lithuania into Russia, and with the US Army warning servicemembers that the Cybertruck is not allowed in Germany.

Nevertheless a few people still manage to get Cybertrucks onto European roads, by getting individual approval from one country or another, then driving across borders. But even in cases like that, a story like this shows that drivers could open themselves up to trouble by driving this unapproved vehicle on European roads.

#4615. November skygazing: Planetary alignments, a supermoon, comet, and more

Published Oct 31, 2026 9:00 AM EDT

Autumn is here! The air is crisp, the leaves are falling, and the sky is alive. November brings a whole gamut of celestial phenomena for stargazing enthusiasts from a  planetary prom to a meteor shower that can explode occasionally into the most spectacular of sky shows, and  a comet that won’t return for 21 years Let’s get to it!

Mercury is generally difficult to spot. It’s our solar system’s smallest planet and is often lost in the sun’s haze. But in the middle of this month, this speedy boy is flitting in to join the party that Venus, Mars, and Jupiter are throwing all month. The three larger planets will be in alignment for all of November, festooning the morning sky just before  dawn. Venus will be in the southeastern sky, with Mars high in the eastern sky and Jupiter a bit lower, but also towards the east. And Mercury? Look low in the southeast, and it should be visible just before the sun emerges over the horizon.

As the month continues, Mars and Jupiter will edge closer and closer to one another, casting shy glances at one another across the sky like teenagers at a school dance. They’ll finally slide in for a waltz just before sunrise on November 16, where their conjunction in the eastern sky will be chaperoned by the bright star Regulus. Look to the east, but make sure you stop looking once the sun begins to peek its way into the firmament. No planetary conjunction is worth cooking your eyes.

And once the music stops and Mars and Jupiter will slip gracefully away, the fireworks will begin. The Leonids will be visible all month, but their peak is predicted for November 18. At that time, their radiant point—the point from which the meteors appear to emerge—will be right next to the two disengaging dancers in the constellation Leo. This shower usually produces 10 to 15 meteors per hour. However, in 1966 it exploded into one of the most spectacular displays of celestial pyrotechnics ever seen, with thousands of meteors visible every minute. So you never know what you might see!

This month’s full moon is the first of three consecutive supermoons. As per the ever-indispensable Farmer’s Almanac, it will reach peak illumination while below the horizon at 9:50 a.m. EST on November 24. When  actually visible, it’ll appear brightest on the evenings of November 23 and 24. This month’s moon takes its name from the industrious, dam-building rodents of North America, whose long summers of hard work start to pay off in November, when they retreat to their lodges to wait out the winter. Several other Indigenous nations have names that also refer to what animals get up to during the fall: the Tlingit call it the Digging Moon, to the Algonquin it’s the Whitefish Moon, while the Dakota and Lakota call it the Deer Rutting Moon.

The final event of November: a visit from Comet 161P/Hartley–IRAS. The space rock  will reach perihelion—the point at which it’s closest to the sun—on November 27. At that point, its magnitude will be about 12, which means you’ll want a decent telescope to spot it. The International Comet Quarterly suggests at least using a telescope with at least a 7.8 inch (20 centimeter) aperture. If you’ve got such an apparatus, look to the east-northeast, just above the horizon.

Remember that you’ll get the best experience gazing up at the stars if you get away from any sources of light pollution. You should also give your eyes plenty of time adjust to the darkness, and review our stargazing tips before heading out into the night.

#4614. Obesity in Your 20s and 30s May Increase Cancer Risk Later in Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Younger adults with obesity may be more likely to develop cancer before midlife than those who maintain a moderate weight, according to a study published on October 26 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

The risk for cancer became higher as weight increased. The highest rates were seen in those with severe obesity and abdominal obesity.

This highlights the potential importance of weight management in the prevention of early onset cancer.

Rates of both obesity and early onset cancer are rising among younger adults globally.

This study analyzed data from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. The researchers identified 6,313,338 adults ages 20 to 39 who had no history of cancer and who underwent standardized national health screenings.

The researchers followed the participants for an average of 11 years.

Body mass index (BMI) was categorized into five groups ranging from underweight to class II obesity using the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for Asian populations. Waist circumference was also measured as an indicator of abdominal adiposity.

During the analysis, the researchers adjusted for various factors such as:

Over the follow-up period, there were 151,893 cases of cancer among the participants. The incidence rate increased progressively based on obesity categories, from 1.84% in “normal-weight” individuals to 2.24% in class I obesity and 2.62% in class II obesity.

The strongest associations were seen in the following cancers:

Obesity was not associated with breast cancer diagnosed before the age of 50.

Ketan Thanki, MD, board certified colorectal surgeon with the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, explained to Healthline that obesity itself causes states that promote cancer formation.

This current study focused on the Korean population. However, the connection between obesity and cancer risk is a global issue.

Previous research has shown that around 10% of all new cancer diagnoses in the United States are associated with obesity. Obesity also accounts for up to 50% of certain cancers, including endometrial and liver cancer.

The study also showed that waist circumference, which indicates abdominal obesity, may be linked to cancer risk that is similar to that of individuals with overweight.

The study researchers used the thresholds set out by the Korean Society for the Study of Obesity. These thresholds put the waist circumference cutoff at over 90 cm (35.4 in) for males and over 85cm (33.46 in) for females.

These are not universal cutoffs. According to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), waist circumference measurements that can increase your risk of negative health issues are 101.6 cm (40 in) for males and 88.9 cm (35 in) for females.

Previous research has also suggested an association between waist circumference and cancer risk, independent of BMI. One study showed a potential 11% increased risk of cancer in people with a waist circumference over the thresholds, even if they were physically active.

The current study found that males had a higher relative association between obesity and cancer, while females showed higher absolute risk.

The researchers also found that the absolute risk was higher in adults ages 30 to 39.

Those who currently smoke or who have ever smoked were also found to have a higher risk of developing cancer than those who have never smoked.

“Diet, exercise, and now medications can all be used very effectively to reduce one’s weight and, hopefully as a result, cancer risk,” Thanki said.

He also noted that, due to differences between South Korean populations and those in other countries such as the United States, further studies will be needed to determine how this translates across other populations.

“But I think this trend will likely extend across all cultures,” he said.

It’s a cute nod to Houston’s space history. It’s also a service area drawn for a meme, and Robotaxi Tracker counts only 34 driverless Model Ys to cover it.

Tesla’s official Robotaxi account announced the expansion on X this morning with “Houston, we have liftoff” and a map comparing the old and new geofences:

Houston, we have liftoff Bigger service area now live pic.twitter.com/ps8fZmWpuP

When Tesla launched in Houston in April, the service covered a small zone of about 25 square miles in northwest Harris County, around Jersey Village, Willowbrook and a stretch of FM 1960. It was miles away from downtown Houston.

The new geofence turns that zone into the nose cone and adds a long body running southeast to downtown and Bellaire, where it flares out into fins. Pair that with “Houston, we have liftoff,” a riff on the famous Apollo 13 line, and the theme isn’t subtle.

The problem is that a long rocket drawn diagonally across a map also looks a lot like something else, and Tesla has been here before. #4611. 3 things you might not know about daylight saving time

Published Oct 31, 2026 1:39 PM EDT

Heads up: The clocks are about to change. The evening of Halloween gets an extra hour as the clocks fall back an hour, meaning you can sleep in on Sunday, November 1.

Complaints about daylight savings are as old as daylight savings itself, and pretty much everyone has an opinion about the practice. As with any such topic, there are all kinds of myths and misunderstandings out there.

This one comes up a lot: the idea that farmers are the reason we have daylight savings. In this version of the story, farmers, who work outside and need to align their workdays with the daylight, were the ones who made the argument for the practice.

In truth, farmers were the main group opposed to daylight savings during World War I. According to the Library of Congress: “The agriculture industry fervently opposed the measure because farming schedules are based on sunrise and sunset not the clock.”

After the war there was a bill to repeal daylight savings, which passed through both houses of Congress. President Woodrow Wilson vetoed that bill, and his statement about the veto acknowledged this wouldn’t make farmers happy.

“I realize the very considerable and in some respects very serious inconveniences to which the daylight-saving law subjects the farmers of the country,” he wrote. Wilson sided with the industrial sector. The veto was overridden, leading to a long period where daylight savings was practiced only in certain areas. For example: New York City observed daylight savings, but rural areas in New York State did not (not what you’d expect if farmers broadly supported daylight savings).

None of this is to say that some farmers don’t support daylight savings time today—it’s just that farmers aren’t the reason the practice exists in America. If anything, they tried to stop it.

There are some “facts” repeated so often that hardly anyone questions them, and “Ben Franklin invented daylight savings time” remains one of them. The problem is that it’s not true.

I’d understand if you’re skeptical—I’m a Canadian journalist trying to steal an achievement from one of America’s founding fathers. But you don’t have to take my word on this one—The Franklin Institute, a museum dedicated to Franklin’s legacy, states that “Daylight saving time is one thing that Franklin did not invent.” The United States didn’t even implement daylight savings until 1918, well over a century after Franklin passed away.

So where did the idea that he invented it come from? Probably from a satirical Journal de Paris article Franklin penned back in 1784.

In that piece he jokingly encouraged the residents of Paris to wake up earlier in the morning, in order to spend less money on candles. He also proposed a tax on shutters, rationing of candles, a prohibition of carriages on the streets after sunset, and church bells ringing at the crack of dawn every day. He, it goes without saying, wasn’t being entirely serious.

So where did the idea for daylight savings come from? New Zealand entomologist George Hudson first proposed intentionally shifting the clock in an 1895 talk to the Wellington Philosophical Society, then followed up with a paper in 1898.

This isn’t a myth, exactly, but it is something that rarely comes up in contemporary discussions about daylight savings. Multiple US states have proposed doing away with standard time entirely. Nationally, the Sunshine Protection Act, which passed the House over the summer, would institute the change from sea to shining sea.

Here’s the thing, though: this isn’t the first time. The US tried making daylight savings permanent during the height of the 1970s energy crisis. The problem was that people hated it. What was supposed to be a two-year experiment lasted less than a year because of a massive change in public opinion.

Support for the change started high, as an October 1974 New York Times article lays out: 79 percent of the public favored the idea in December of 1973, but by February of 1974, that dropped to 42 percent—a 37-point swing. A bill to restore standard time in winter passed the House by a 362 to 16 vote.

What caused the backlash? Dark winter mornings. Particularly prominent were complaints from parents, who didn’t like their children walking to school in the dark.

A 1975 study by the US Department of Transportation concluded that a year-round switch possibly isn’t a great idea, proposing instead a schedule change. “We conclude that modest overall benefits might be realized by a shift from the historic 6-month DST system (May through October) to an 8-month DST system (March through October),” the paper concludes. This, notably, is pretty much what the US has been doing since 2007.

The past isn’t a prediction of the future—it’s possible switching to year-round daylight savings would go differently today. Walking to school is less common, for one thing, and streets are better lit. All the same, it’s worth realizing this has been tried before.

#4610. Letter From the Editor-in-Chief: What a Decade of Bedtime Stories Taught Me About Health

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

I’ve read to my children each night at bedtime for as long as I (and they) can remember. We started with the likes of “Goodnight Batcave” and the lesser-known-in-the-US but oh-so-wonderful collection of verse-driven classics from former UK Children’s Laureate Julia Donaldson.

We moved on to B.J. Novak’s anarchic love letter to the power of words (and to great typography), “The Book With No Pictures.”

We eventually worked our way up to Roald Dahl’s wickedly dark back catalog, discovering more complex characters, language and plotting as we went.

When my eldest, Amelia, hit 6, it was time to roll out the big guns.

Over the last 5 years (she’s now 11), I’ve read the seven Harry Potter books aloud twice, complete with all the voices: once to Amelia on her own, once to both her and her brother, Henry, two years her junior.

I had feared she wouldn’t be keen on another helping, but Amelia immersed herself once more in the world of Hogwarts with no hesitation and took immense joy in watching Henry discover for himself every twist and turn on Harry’s journey.

We have done the same thing with Tolkien’s “The Hobbit” and his fantasy masterpiece “The Lord of the Rings,” and are currently midway through “The Two Towers” on our second go around.

There’s a huge amount of reciprocal joy we take from this nightly ritual, beyond the practical benefits of providing a calming demarcation between the end of the day and the wind-down to sleep.

For me, it comes as either a break in my working day or a signal that it’s over, depending on how hectic things are.

For the kids, it’s an all-too-rare chance to get me all to themselves, no deadlines, screens, or other distractions to pull me away from being anything but 100% present.

For all three of us, it’s a literal (and literary!) warm blanket — a chance to escape under the covers to familiar worlds and familiar faces. It is, in short, incredibly good for our well-being.

And yet, in the world of health information — including on this site — thousands, if not millions, of reading hours are dedicated to the benefits of nutrition, sleep, and exercise as the building blocks of good health. Reading itself rarely makes that shortlist.

For me, it unequivocally deserves a place on it. Research seems to support that case. Even if we need more of it to really understand how and why.

A recent editorial in Psychological Medicine co-authored by Barbara Sahakian, Professor of Clinical Neuropsychology at Cambridge University, draws on a broad range of research linking reading for pleasure to better mental health and greater empathy.

The positive impact of reading on young people — just like Amelia and Henry — lso carries evidence.

Among more than 10,000 US adolescents, those who started reading for pleasure early had fewer mental health problems, spent less time on screens and slept more. Although, per an earlier column of mine, I can’t vouch for the sleep side of things when it comes to early bird Henry.

For many, reading can be a form of therapy that improves well-being. Bibliotherapy is a complementary therapeutic tool for emotional release and reduced stress and anxiety, with its roots traced back to ancient civilizations.

There’s even research suggesting a link between a love of reading and a lower risk of cognitive decline.

In a 2003 study of people aged 75 and over, reading was associated with a 35% lower risk of dementia over roughly five years.

A separate 14-year study from 2022 found that people who read at least weekly saw less cognitive decline, whatever their level of education.

A happy (and healthy) by-product of this love of being read to is that both my kids have now started reading to me at bedtime. Henry recently read “Jeffy the Burglar’s Cat” to us, a lesser-known but no less compelling chapter book by Ursula Moray Williams that was a staple of my own childhood. And we’ve enjoyed several books from Amelia, including the wistful tale of friendship and the circle of life, “Charlotte’s Web” by E.B. White – not a dry eye in the house for the final few chapters of that one.

They’ve also gone off and re-read the Harry Potter books and “The Hobbit” to themselves.

The research above links reading to many health benefits: better attention and memory, fewer mental health problems, more sleep, less time on screens, and greater empathy. I haven’t measured any of those impacts empirically in our house. Nor am I naive to the fact that as they get older, they’ll ultimately grow out of me reading to them, with school, extracurricular activities, their friends, and inevitably screens competing for more and more of their time.

Come what may, though, I know that a child who considers missing a reading session as the most cardinal of cardinal sins, and who scrambles for the chance to read aloud to their dad at bedtime is, at that moment, concentrating, empathizing, discovering and growing.

Researchers are clear that studies espousing the benefits of reading show association rather than proof, and it’s evident that more experimental work and deeper research are needed to ensure the complex cause and effect stands on firm scientific ground.

Regardless, it’s a healthy habit Amelia, Henry and I are very happy to keep, and with a bit of luck, I’ll get to pass it on to their kids one day.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4606. What to do if you hit a deer

Published Oct 31, 2026 2:07 PM EDT

When you think of the fall season, chances are that gorgeous foliage, brisk sweater weather, and Halloween decorations come to mind. Deer, on the other hand, think of sex.

Deer breeding behavior, known as the rut, aligns with the changing length of daylight. As daylight decreases, buck (male deer) and doe (female deer) hormones increase. While in southern states the rut can last several months, it only runs for a short period of time during the fall in the Northeast.

During the rut, bucks seek out does that are ready to breed, and the amorous pursuit can be intense. Because some bucks are so obsessed with breeding, they can eat little and burn through up to 20 percent of their body weight during the season. And just like love-crazed high schoolers, deer during the rut are more distracted and less cautious, as well as more active during the day than they usually are.

“During this period, many yearling bucks leave their birth areas in search of new territory, sometimes dozens of miles away. At the same time, adult bucks are actively roaming their home ranges in pursuit of doe, often chasing those they encounter,” according to Raven Ridge Wildlife Center in Pennsylvania.

What’s more, “The end of daylight-saving time means more vehicles will be on the road during dusk and dawn, which are the peak hours for deer movement.”

In fact, most deer-vehicle accidents take place in October through December. While there are things you can do to lessen your chances of hitting one—such as staying alert and paying close attention when you see deer crossing signs—sometimes accidents are unavoidable. So what should you do if you hit a deer?

Safely pull over and turn your emergency flashers on. While your instinct might be to go see the deer or move the body off of the road, resist the temptation. Care for any injured passengers, and call 911. The dispatchers will send the appropriate authorities to help.

And if you narrowly avoided one deer, remember that, “deer often travel in groups and walk single file,” per the Raven Ridge Wildlife Center. “So even if one deer successfully crosses the road in front of a driver, it doesn’t mean the threat is over. Another could be right behind it.”

#4604. Putrid blood shoots from these lizards’ eyes

Published Nov 1, 2026 8:03 AM EST

Horned lizards are spiky cuties. Three to six inches long, these lizards are coated with sharp spines all across their hard, sand-colored backs. But in the dry deserts and prairies they call home, they are still vulnerable. As they scuttle through the protective brush in arid landscapes from Mexico to southern Canada, they have to reckon with hungry coyotes, snakes that will gobble them whole, and even peckish roadrunners. That’s why multiple species of horned lizards have developed a weird but effective deterrent: blood.

And not just any blood: These lizards shoot foul-smelling blood out of their eyes, sending many would-be predators scattering. But experts say the lizards are now facing other threats to their survival that even a fountain of eye blood can’t deter.

Dean Williams, a professor of biology at Texas Christian University, studies horned lizard populations in central Texas. He says that blood squirting is really a backup defense for the lizards. “Their first line of defense is going to be crypsis,” aka blending in with their background, says Williams.

Williams and his colleagues tag the lizards they study with radio trackers that pinpoint their location to an area roughly the size of an office desk. Even then, he says, it can take “15 minutes of rummaging” to find the lizard in their scrubland habitat. The lizards don’t move much, he added, blending in with nearby rocks.

But when hiding doesn’t work, the lizards deploy their unusual, foul-smelling blood, which Williams says is a product of an equally foul delicacy. “Their diet consists mainly of these large Pogonomyrmex or harvester ants,” says Williams. Harvester ants defend themselves using neurotoxic venom that causes intense, long-lasting, stinging pain in mammals.

Unfortunately for the harvester ants, this toxin doesn’t even slightly deter horned lizards, who eat the ants in large numbers. A 2024 study identified that a compound in the lizards’ blood spiked after scientists fed them harvester ants. The researchers think this compound, possibly adapted from ant venom, makes the lizards’ blood taste foul.

However, that gross metabolized ant blood coursing through the lizards’ veins wouldn’t be much help if it only annoyed a predator after it had already bitten off the lizard’s head. That’s where the lizards’ unusual squirting mechanism comes in handy.

Williams explains that the lizards can build up pressure in blood vessels around their sinuses. Eventually, the vessels burst, shooting the toxic blood out in jets. Mammals exposed to the stream of blood react with notable disgust. There seems to be little consequence for the lizards, even though in one experiment, a lizard lost 6.8 percent of its body mass after squirting blood when exposed to a dog.

The foul-smelling blood doesn’t protect the lizards from every predator, though. Roadrunners and other birds of prey still chow down on them, says Williams. To guard against birds, the lizards use the sharp horns on the back of their heads to stab at predators that try to seize them in their beaks.

The lizards’ foul blood also does little to deter snakes. Instead, the lizards have evolved specialized strategies to evade these predators. Rattlesnakes are lazy hunters that wait in the shadows for prey to approach. Horned lizards have learned to run away from these snakes.

But Williams says they use a different strategy if hunted by a coachwhip or racer snake. These fearsome snakes can easily chase down the lizards, who instead quickly flatten their bodies against the dirt, showing the snake their spiked backs, which makes them harder to swallow.

But despite these bespoke, often ingenious defense mechanisms, horned lizards in the Lone Star State are under serious threat. They’ve disappeared from their habitat across eastern Texas. Williams says that industrialization is devastating lizard populations. “They seem to be very sensitive to those habitat changes,” he says.

In small towns, the lizards can live alongside humans when their natural brush habitat is preserved. But in towns where humans cleared the brush, “the lizards just disappeared,” Williams says.

Horned lizards are ectotherms, meaning they must change their behavior to keep their body temperature under control. In the blistering heat of a Texas summer, the lizards simply can’t keep their bodies within safe limits once the cool shade of vegetation has disappeared.

Harvester ants provide horned lizards with one of their strongest defenses. But another ant species has become the second major challenge to the lizards’ survival. Fire ants are an invasive species in the United States. They swarm the nests of ground-dwelling lizards, eating vulnerable eggs, or even attacking and killing young lizards.

That’s where conservation efforts, like the one Williams works on with zoos across Texas, play an important role. The program releases nearly a thousand young lizards each year.

These hatchlings, which can easily fit in the palm of a hand, are packaged in individual Tupperware containers and then released in the desert scrub. Williams says that his graduate student, Kira Gangbin, has been working on a targeted poison to cut down fire ant numbers and help keep these hatchlings alive. These efforts will hopefully keep horned lizard populations thriving for many more years. Just remember: If you come across a horned lizard on a hike through the Texas desert, give it a wide berth, or risk a foul, bloody surprise.

#4603. How Non-Dairy Creamers Doubled Coffee’s Calories For Many Americans

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Coffee consumption among U.S. adults remained relatively stable between 2003 and 2018, but the average number of calories consumed from coffee beverages increased by nearly 40%, according to a study published in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.

By 2017–2018, U.S. adults consumed an average of about 13 ounces of coffee beverages per day. Meanwhile, the average daily calorie intake from these beverages had increased from 43 to 60 calories since 2003–2004.

By 2018, non-dairy creamer had become the largest source of calories added to coffee, surpassing sugar or syrup and dairy milk.

The researchers analyzed data from eight consecutive cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 2003 to 2018. The study included 30,459 U.S. adults ages 20 and older who provided two 24-hour dietary recalls.

The researchers categorized coffee beverages based on whether they contained added ingredients. These additions included:

The researchers found that coffee intake remained stable, while the average calorie intake from coffee beverages increased.

The absolute increase in caloric intake is about 17 kcal per day, which is only about 1% of a 2,000 kcal diet.

Coffee consumption was also higher among men, non-Hispanic white adults, and people with higher incomes. Those who slept fewer hours or worked longer hours also tended to drink more coffee.

In 2018, the most common coffee additions by weight were:

The researchers found no significant changes in the amounts of dairy milk, sugar or syrup, and sugar substitutes added to coffee between 2003 and 2018.

However, consumption of non-dairy additions increased during this period. Non-dairy creamer consumption rose from 3.37 to 8.08 grams per day, while non-dairy milk increased from 0.27 to 2.45 grams per day.

By 2017–2018, non-dairy creamer contributed the most calories among coffee additions:

In 2003–2004, non-dairy creamer contributed an average of 7.7 calories per day, meaning its calorie contribution more than doubled by 2017–2018.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, president of KAK, Consulting, LLC, and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Cleveland, Ohio, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings didn’t surprise her.

“The variety of coffee drinks, both at coffee houses and grocery stores, as well as options for creamers in the grocery store, make it easy to trade in black coffee for something closer to dessert,” she said.

She also added, however, that not all non-dairy creamers are created equal.

“Some are quite natural, with minimal ingredients, including no added sugars and no additives. Others are ingredient-heavy with either a large amount of sugar (real or artificial) and additives, so it’s really based on the type that is purchased,” she noted.

More than 60% of Americans drink coffee daily. Research suggests that drinking coffee with little to no added sugar or saturated fat may offer health benefits.

Previous research has associated moderate coffee consumption, typically around 3–5 cups per day, with a lower risk of several health conditions, including:

“These benefits make sense. After all, coffee beans are indeed a deeply hued plant, with multiple bioactive compounds that may strengthen health,” said Kirkpatrick.

She also cautioned consumers to be mindful of any caffeine sensitivities they may have. However, the benefits of coffee have been seen in studies assessing both caffeinated and decaf options.

However, adding ingredients high in sugar or saturated fat could offset some of coffee’s potential health benefits.

Kirkpatrick noted that some studies suggest milk may enhance antioxidant activity. The current study did not examine whether coffee additions reduced its health benefits, but found that these ingredients contributed additional calories.

Other research has raised concerns about the potential health effects of consuming excessive added sugar and certain food additives.

“I suggest that my patients try to embrace a black cup of coffee as opposed to starting the day with sugar,” Kirkpatrick said.

She suggested that certain additions, such as chicory root or cinnamon, may enhance your brew while still providing benefits. Plain milk can also provide protein and calcium without added sugar.

“Starting the day with [something] sweet may make it difficult to limit sugary foods later in the day. Starting the day with a more bitter approach may [be] an important factor in keeping sugar down, as bitter compounds may positively impact appetite-regulating pathways,” said Kirkpatrick.

#4602. Battlefield 6 patch finally ends the menace of the Lock-Guided Missile, shuts down the Recon Drone Sledgehammer exploit and more

Today's Battlefield 6 patch is laser-focused on taking care of some of the more infuriating bugs while also taking out a couple of exploits.

The next Battlefield 6 update is here. Having gone live just moments ago, update 1.1.1.5 is something of a midseason update, bringing a few quality of life tweaks to the game alongside some key fixes for a few of the issues that cropped up since the launch of Season 1 in late October.

This latest release is also the first to tackle some of the problems players have been running into playing Redsec battle royale, the free-to-play component that also came out recently.

Patch 1.1.1.5 is fairly limited in scope. The biggest fix in this one comes to the Lock-Guided Missiles going through flares, and generally being annoying enough to stop players from using air vehicles altogether.

The Lock-Guided Missiles were mainly used by AA vehicles, but they could also be equipped by IFVs, which made it even more of a nightmare to pilots. It got so bad that Battlefield Studios disabled it entirely while the team worked on a proper fix.

Another exploit the patch fixes is the one that allowed players to stand on the Recon Drone and reach areas they’re not supposed to. This was done by… repeatedly hitting it with a Sledgehammer. The long-running issue of vehicles not spawning for certain teams in Conquest and Breakthrough appears to have finally been fixed, too.

In terms of battle royale, the patch has a few fixes that should help make the experience more consistent, as well as improve the flow of matches. One of the more interesting addresses an issue that could eliminate the entire squad instead of reviving dead teammates when using a Mobile Spawn.

Patch 1.1.1.5 also has yet more adjustments to weapon dispersion (bloom). Some of the casses it addresses include transitioning from sprint to firing in ADS, and others where it apparently scaled with player movement speed.

BMW’s new iX5 is hard to miss with its distinct Double-X headlights. Here’s how it stacks up against the outgoing X5, side by side.

The X5 is among BMW’s best-selling vehicles in the US. In its fifth generation, it will be available across five powertrains.

In the US, it will be offered in gas, plug-in hybrid (PHEV), and, for the first time, battery electric (EV) powertrains. Other markets will also see diesel and hydrogen fuel cell variants.

The gas-powered 2027 X5 40 xDrive is now available, starting at $72,100, but the electric iX5 won’t go on sale until November.

Ahead of its official launch next month, Bimmertoday posted several images of the new iX5 parked next to the outgoing X5 G05, giving us a good side-by-side comparison.

Although it still looks like an X5, the new iX5 stands apart with BMW’s Neue Klasse design. The new upright, slimmer BMW Kidney Grille replaces the old wide, chunkier grille design.

A post shared by bimmertoday (@bimmertoday)

You can also see BMW’s new “double-X” light signature, which combines the headlights, daytime running lights, side lights, and turn signals into one unit. The Double-X headlights come standard, but BMW said you can turn them off for simpler diagonal stripes.

BMW’s new iX5 is 197.2″ long, 78.7″ wide, and 68.9″ tall, or about the size of the Porsche Cayenne Electric.

#4600. Fierce turtles square off in a rare woodland turf battle

Published Nov 1, 2026 10:10 AM EST

At first, it appears that two turtles with yellow spots are calmly sitting side by side. Suddenly, one of them turns, slowly—and lunges out with its head, its open beak clearly trying to take an aggressive chomp out of its neighbor. Moments later, the turtle tries again. Now, both reptiles are going head-to-head, though each is retracted into the protection of its shell.

The two combatants are male eastern box turtles (Terrapene carolina carolina) competing for dominance. Eastern box turtles are a subspecies of the common box turtle (Terrapene carolina), with bright orange and yellow coloring on its dark shell. They live throughout the eastern and midwestern United States.

“I wouldn’t say that they’re normally aggressive, but male box turtles can definitely become territorial, especially since males’ home ranges (the area they frequently occupy) often overlap,” Eamon Caffrey, the turtle research coordinator at Mass Audubon who captured the video, tells Popular Science. “We do occasionally see this sort of brawling behavior between two males when out in the field; you just have to get lucky enough to actually witness it. This experience was a first for me, and I was thrilled to capture it on camera.”

Over the summer, another Mass Audubon staff member saw two male box turtles opting for a pushing contest instead of biting. At one point, one of the two flipped the other contestant onto its back and pushed him down a small hill. Box turtle battles can also feature spinning each other around.

“From my understanding, fights between male box turtles are much more opportunistic than anything else,” Caffrey tells Popular Science. “Often, when two males come in contact, they will display a variety of aggressive behaviors that can include head butting, shell ramming, biting, pushing, and shoving – all in attempts to assert dominance. These disputes are often territorial but can be over mates as well.”

What’s more, the turtle with the darker shell is a well-known individual over 30 years old. Caffrey says he’s seen him various times this year, and since capturing the video the celebrity reptile has been spending time in an area where the Mass Audubon team frequently spot two to three adult females. However, there’s been no trace of his opponent.

“Does that mean he ‘won’ the battle?” Caffrey muses. “Who knows.”
